en: The first chapter, titled "The Section on the Application of Questions. Om! Salutation to Mahābhairava, to the deities of the directions and others, and to the gurus.
On the delightful peak of Jyotiṣka, variegated with various minerals, filled with diverse trees and creepers, and crowded with many sages.
Crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and served by the Gaṇas and Pramathas, all the lords of the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra—gathered there.
Seeing Bhairava in a state of joy, they addressed Ambikā: "You are the mother of this world; you alone are my refuge. (3)
O you of great renown, you are the savior of those terrified by the fear of saṃsāra; [so too are] the ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, hosts of vidyādharas, and others. ||4||
Terrified by old age and death in this wheel of saṃsāra, other living beings as well—afflicted and fearing [further] aging and death—have gone to you alone for refuge. (5)

Ask Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods and the benefactor of the world, about the true nature that is the essence of all knowledge and the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having heard their words—by which [knowledge] they are liberated and by contentment with which they achieve success—the Goddess spoke these words.
Having praised the Lord Maheśāna with hymns that describe his true nature—she who is the mother of creation, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śakti, and likewise Ambikā—[one should proceed].
Raudrī is the power who sustains the universe; such is her function and her essential nature. Thus the Supreme Goddess is praised through this hymn of praise.

I bow to that Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the master of all the lords of the worlds, who is partless yet possesses all portions, whose effects—consisting of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vikārā, renowned for their qualities, and characterized by sovereignty and power—are most stable like a pillar; he who has fashioned the entire collection of the creation of the principles (tattvas) and so forth, yet remains beyond all states of being, devoid of the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva.
"O Lord, I have heard the Tantras which are secret and whose domain is hidden; the paths of the Left and the Right, and the Yāmalas in their many forms. (11)
And the Siddhāntas, O Lord of the Gods, are divided into ten and eighteen types; they further branch into hundreds of millions, and indeed into many millions in manifold ways.
In the *Siddhayogeśvarītantra*, which extends over a hundred million verses, two sūtras have emerged from the root-tantra, the great sūtra. (13)
Among those, one alone has been understood by me as originating from the ocean of wombs; I have not heard the supreme *Tantrasadbhāva*, which I now desire to hear.
In that regard, O Lord, there are many kinds of conduct, ritual action, knowledge, and yoga; furthermore, there are various types of *dhāraṇā*, both with seed (*sabījā*) and without seed (*nirbījā*).
The generation directed toward the Self occurs through the union of manifold means; it resides in the Nāda, is established in the Bindu, abides in the movement, and traverses the six paths.

O God, that which has entered the utterance of power (śakti), which reaches the abandonment of causes and time, and another which has entered the state of emptiness—this [power] resides in the heart, established in power. || 17 ||

It is situated at the end of the twelve, yet it abides on the path while being devoid of the path; it resides in the emission (visarga), is established within the eternal, and is stationed in the Brahma-nāḍī. || 18 ||

Furthermore, [he meditated upon] the Supreme God beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), within the interior of the gateway of Brahman; likewise, he meditated upon the Yoga situated in emergence and the one situated in separation for the wielder of the trident.
I wish to understand this which abides in dissolution and that which transcends dissolution; furthermore, O Lord, how do they all again attain a single state of being? (20)
O Lord of the Gods, tell me how they exist when they have become liquefied, and what is the power of the mantras which is the cause of their accomplishment.
Therefore, O God, best of the gods, for what reason have those mantras which were previously spoken by you as granters of the fulfillment of desires been concealed once again? (22)
Why do those [mantras] numbering seventy million not succeed for each of the animal-sacrifices, even when performed according to the ritual manual (kalpa)? || 23 ||

O Lord of the World, O Lord of the Gods, human beings undergo extreme suffering for the sake of liberation; yet how can there be liberation or spiritual attainment here for those who are devoid of mantra? (24)
O Lord of Gods, the syllables, protected by that imperishable power known as Vāmā who is the mother of all mantras, have attained the state of absolute liberation.
How is that subtle, supreme aspect, whose form is radiant energy, known? For just as the burning power of fire exists even while its rays shine forth. || 26 ||
In exactly the same way, it is also figuratively designated as a quality (*dharma*) of Śiva; by virtue of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), it is figuratively applied everywhere. (27)
Śakti is not devoid of Śiva, nor is Śiva devoid of Śakti; their separation is never observed, just like that of the wind and the sky.
Through his power, which functions as the instrument, Śiva’s activity proceeds; there is no other instrument for him by which he might perform that activity. (29)
The mantra is declared to be Śiva, and its constituent phonemes are the designators of that very [Śiva]. Through the union of the signified and the signifier, Śiva is thus recited.
In this matter, O Lord, from where has your power departed, having abandoned Maheśvara, such that your mantras of immeasurable splendor have become fruitless? (31)
But how was the Mātṛkā born, she who is the mother of mantras? And how is she the mother of the universe, she whose form is mantra? (32)
"Tell me that which is the source of all the *khecarīs*. Śrī Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate lady, that you have indeed questioned me!
I shall tell you all of that; listen, O long-eyed one, to those tantras—left, right, and yāmala—which have been recounted by me.
Likewise, O Goddess, there are the divisions of Rudra and the divisions of Śiva; therein, O leader of the gods, are conduct, ritual action, yoga, and knowledge. (35)
In that regard, all those who were questioned here and there were led astray; the knowledge was not explained to them out of consideration for the fluctuations of their minds. || 36 ||
O Goddess, whatever was desired by each [seeker], that I have explained accordingly, through mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and other difficult yogas. (37)
O Dear One, by means of many methods such as exhaling, inhaling, and meditating, people are led astray by the expansion of ritual actions; I have not taught [true] knowledge.
But they, out of pride in their own knowledge, questioned him with contempt: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Candra, and Prajāpati. (39)
All the hosts of Skanda and Nandi, as well as Śukra and the other yogis—all of them have accomplished their purpose, as has whatever else was undertaken.
O lady of excellent hips, that very knowledge—which provides every means and is endowed with immediate conviction—is not grasped by those of dull intellect. (41)
O leader of the gods, out of affection for you, I shall explain in brief the bliss of the Yoginī-hṛdaya, which has come down through the lineage of succession.
A living being has three principal channels: Suṣumṇā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā. These extend upwards and downwards, pervaded by the vital breath joined with the individual soul.
Below the navel there is a knot, having the appearance of a hen’s egg; its stalk extends upward for a distance of one span (vitasti).
Above that, there should be an eight-petaled lotus, white and reddish.
It is surrounded by sixteen filaments, each four finger-breadths wide; the pericarp likewise has a circumference of one finger-breadth. 46.
It should be square at the base and broad; it is proclaimed to have the form of a water-pot and to resemble Mount Meru.
Situated in the center of that [lotus], the individual soul (jīva) dwells in happiness like Śiva; it is as subtle as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, atomic in form, and exceedingly pure.
It shines with brilliance like lightning and revolves like the orb of the sun; that Supreme Self, residing within the body, is meditated upon by yogis. 49.

That very [bindu] is called the *bindu*; pervading all, it remains established. When non-pervasive and situated in the state of a bound soul (*paśubhāva*), it wanders through the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
Sadāśiva, whose nature is primordial impurity and māyā yet is eternally liberated, creates various bonds consisting of the qualities (guṇas) characterized by existence and non-existence.
Those qualities exist as being bound, residing within the atom; therefore, in this way, the point (bindu) should be joined to its own nature within the non-existents.
The drop (bindu) is declared to be the Self; the Self is remembered as the drop. The supreme drop is all-pervasive, established in that which transcends dissolution. || 53 ||
Having then understood the two drops, he is liberated from saṃsāra; it is endowed with four parts and has the form of a spark of fire.
The Lord Īśa abides in the heart-lotus, O leader of the gods; he remains within the womb of Māyā like a flash of lightning amidst its radiance.
Having the appearance of a serpent asleep in its coils, she abides in a curved form; therefore she is called Kuṇḍalinī, being the very nature of consciousness of the Self. 56.
O beautiful lady, by her that living soul is led upward and downward; she is indeed declared to be Māyā, the Kuṇḍalinī who revolves counter-clockwise.
The second, however, is named Jyeṣṭhā; it is remembered as a straight line, having a form resembling a lotus fiber, and it sets in motion the path of emanation.
Raudrī is proclaimed as the third, having the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭaka); the fourth is Nirodhī, having the form of a crescent moon.
The group of four is recited as consisting of Will, Knowledge, Action, and Pervasiveness; the fifth is the power of Śiva, which effects coming and going.
One should generate the desire for the arising of the intellect; that which performs volition is to be known as threefold: characterized by goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).
Likewise, the power of knowledge and knowledge itself consist of eight types: the fourfold set of virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya). || 62 ||
Likewise, unrighteousness, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of mastery—as well as knowledge divided into eight kinds—produces and transforms [the elements]. (63)
Both conceptualization and discursive thought function for the sake of worldly activity; it is action alone that performs everything—both merit and demerit—for the bound soul.
Vibhvī, however, should be known as the awakener, the one who awakens the power of consciousness (cicchakti). That which is remembered as the fifth power has its support established therein. (65)
The supreme Śakti is indeed one alone, yet she appears as infinitefold through the diversity of her actions; by her power, O Dear One, [beings] enjoy virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. (66)

And this is the mental creation, consisting of the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas); within it, righteousness and so forth belong to the creation of goodness, while unrighteousness and so forth belong to that of darkness.
Rajas causes agitation for both of them; therefore, it gives birth to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Intellect, mind, and ego are known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka); likewise, there are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya are known as the supports of the vital breaths (prāṇa); the channels (nāḍīs), moreover, are supported by that [breath]. (70)
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third; Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā as well as Yaśā. (71)
Alambuṣā, Kuhū by name, and Śāṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth; with these, O highly fortunate lady, the heart-lotus always remains.
The deity beginning with Brahmā is denoted by the syllable *akāra*; that *akāra*, having become twofold, performs its function therein.
Desire dissolves into knowledge, and knowledge, in turn, through action; action dissolves into the pervasive power, and the pervasive power becomes one with Śiva.
Established in the state of Brahman, each [element] dissolves into its own respective place; having withdrawn all its own effects, Brahmā departs.
Where the letter *i* stands as the supreme abode and Viṣṇu resides, there sound is dissolved, withdrawing its own effects. (76)
Brahmā, with his neck dissolved, is situated in the anterior support; the supreme station of Viṣṇu is there, where the letter *i* is established. (77)
One should know that place where Viṣṇu goes as far as Rudra and where the syllable *oṃ* abides, extending to the palate, as the path of coming and going for all living beings.
When Rudra also enters into Īśvara, the letter *ma* remains there; that is designated as Nirodhā, situated above Lambakā. (79)
Because she obstructs the upward path, she is proclaimed as Raudrī; above that, the target born of Nāda is there, and the letter *M* goes to that place.
That place where the emergence of Nāda occurs is declared to be the abode of Śiva; and above the Lambaka, O beloved, are those two Bindus.

O beautiful lady, that is said to end with the visarga, and it is also the twelve-finger limit (dvādaśānta); it is remembered as ending with the kalās, ending with the vowels, and ending with the sixteen.
And where sound arises, when Raudrī becomes divided, even the Nāda goes, O Goddess, to where Kuṇḍalikā is situated.

O Dear One, one should know that it does not end with the *nāda*, but extends beyond the *visarga*. Above that is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which is the upward-flowing stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and the state of Manonmanī.
O Goddess, within that pervasive Lord, Manonmanī is dissolved; there, O Dear One, the Sphoṭa arises from the mouth of the Guru below.
Above that is the mouth of the Guru, which is remembered as the station of Brahmā; that is also remembered as the station of Śakti, and it is called the end of dissolution (layānta). || 86 ||
At its end, however, it is said to be beyond dissolution; of this there is no doubt. O fair-faced one, such is the movement of the *bindu* for those who are awakened. 87.
But those who are unawakened, O Goddess, and are obstructed by Nirodhinī—for them, the state of rebirth as an animal is declared, which binds one to the existence of saṃsāra. (88)
This movement is always declared to be "active" (pravṛtta); however, I shall further explain its cessation, which will result in the abandonment of the womb. || 89 ||
Having abandoned the five causes, one attains the state of moving according to one's own will; this is the yoga consisting of the *bindu*, when one desires to renounce [the world]. (90)
Then, O Goddess, he shall possess the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā*; when his renunciation has reached the station of Brahman, O beautiful one. (91)
Then he attains oneness with Brahman, as well as sound and touch; having abandoned those two, he abandons even the cause of the Lotus-born One.
Brahmā, whose form is that of the effect, departs when his own task is concluded; he goes to dissolution within the principle of Viṣṇu along with his instruments for performing his duties.

Even Janārdana, when he abides in the supreme Keśava, must be abandoned; for when the states associated with the objects of the senses have been relinquished, he too is relinquished—of this there is no doubt.
Keśava also attains dissolution in Rudra when his mind has abandoned its activity; having ceased from his office, that Keśava is one who perceives the qualities (guṇas).
Endowed with qualities beyond measure, the subtle atom (aṇu) abides in Rudra; Rudra, too, goes into the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign whose form is splendor.
That is declared to be the station of the Bindu; one should point out the mass of splendor, as well as its division consisting of light and the very function of the sense of smell. (97)

Having abandoned these two, one proceeds upward through the functional states of the qualities (guṇavṛttayaḥ) of Rudra; likewise, even Īśvara [is transcended] in the Sound (nāda) called Śabda, which belongs to Sadāśiva.
Engaged in the locus of the intellect and endowed with the qualities of egoism, the Lord likewise proceeds, having well-restrained his own activities.
Wherever the Lord Sadāśiva— the repository of the qualities of auspicious knowledge—
resides, there the Supreme Lord, the knower of wisdom, abides in the highest state.
Having withdrawn its own function, it indeed goes to its own dissolution;
then, having gradually abandoned that supreme state which transcends dissolution, it departs. || 101 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the fourth, Īśvara— all of them, assuming forms for the sake of action, depart, each taking his own quality with him.
May they all be absorbed in Śivā, their physical forms withdrawn by their own power;
for will, knowledge, and action are the instruments of them all.
O fair-faced one, the process of re-absorption has been described here as before; likewise, it occurs separately for emergence, conjunction, and dissolution. (104)

O Queen of the Gods, the supreme power (parā-śakti) which transcends the state of dissolution (layātītā), she who is all-pervasive and of the nature of Śiva— therein, as the support, they move in successive stages.
Even the Lord Sadāśiva performs withdrawal by his own will, O lady of beautiful hips; he is the Bindu of the mind, that which is consciousness on the Great Path.
As soon as that [bond] is withdrawn, the body stands like a piece of wood;
at that moment, the bondage consisting of dharma and adharma is destroyed, without a doubt. || 107 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, when that [ego] has perished, one goes to the supreme state,
O fair-faced one, as long as one is not released from these great bonds.
Until then, how can there be liberation for him, even when the sixfold path has been purified?
Thus, O Goddess, I have proclaimed this renunciation through the Vidyā below.
O Goddess, when Śiva also departs, endowed with all his qualities, he goes to where that Kuṇḍalinī power resides— she who is beyond the mind and is the state of Manonmanī.
Endowed with the three powers, she is to be known as the Awakener and the Obstructer; the Downward-moving is the Restrainer, and the Upward-moving is the Fully Awakener.
For that one [power], having entered into a twofold state, manifests an infinity in the diversity of its functions, creating the entire universe as far as the world of Brahmā.
And he should withdraw [the world] without doubt through the differentiation of his activities, O Pārvatī;
first, in the form of Vāmā, he creates, and as the support of Jyeṣṭhā, he protects.
Withdrawal occurs through the fierce form; O Dear One, she who is one is threefold, and she is said to be fivefold, as well as eightfold and ninefold.
Divided into fifty varieties, she has reached a state of infinite infinity;
she alone, O Vīranāyikā, is to be known in her supreme form.
O beloved, this entire remainder of whatever constitutes speech is pervaded by her;
therefore she is called Māyā, yet Kuṇḍalī is to be known as the very form of the knowable.

Therein, O Goddess, one becomes attained to the state beyond mind (unmanā), free from mental constructs, endowed with the eightfold qualities, and possessed of omniscience and other such attributes. || 117 ||
O Goddess, those elements which exist through their causes—by them this [universe] becomes conjoined;
yet even she, O Beloved, goes to dissolution in the void of the aperture, within the lotus-natured state.
But that place of the Lotus-born is beyond the mind and is hollow; therein the subtle soul, united with it, being liberated, has its own duties brought to completion.

Above that, however, is known the all-pervading one, who is beyond qualities yet the source of qualities; he is both insentient and perfectly conscious, transcending the qualities—thus say those seeking liberation.
That Śiva is supreme liberation, transcending all conceptual construction; he is beyond both merit and demerit, the supreme bringer of bliss to all. || 121 ||
O Dear One, by this sequential method, yoga consisting of the *bindu* should be understood by the wise; it has thus been described in brief. (122)
[The State of Sound] Hereafter I shall explain that which abides in sound; listen to me regarding that which abides in sound.
Sound is to be known as Kuṇḍalinī, established in the center of the navel. 123.
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and abandoned the five causes, she has ascended upwards, having pierced the hierarchy from Brahma up to Śiva.
O fair-faced one, having abandoned her duty in each of their respective stations—namely knowledge, action, and will—she departed from those of Brahmā and the others. (125)
Having grasped the bindu of the mind, she emerged into the fivefold void,
resembling the autumnal moon and blazing like ten million flashes of lightning.
It should be known as having the luster of the rays of the rising sun, resembling a sprout of coral, like a thread of wool, or like the fiber of a lotus stalk. || 127 ||
Then, like the rays of the cool-rayed moon in autumn or like a crest of flame, there appeared before him a drop in the form of a spark of fire. || 128 ||
O Goddess, like a drop of dew upon a lotus petal,
having grasped it in such a manner, one should sever the remaining bond.
Then, standing in the sky, one should gradually draw up the water residing within the lotus-stalk from the heart by means of the exhalation (visarga).
In the same way, O beloved, the yogi should draw up the wind from the heart located within the body, so that it moves without interruption like a lamp placed in a windless spot. 131.
In the same way, O Goddess, the mind should be made to rest on the support of Śakti alone;
when all other causes have been abandoned, one then attains the state of Rudra. || 132 ||
Then, O lady of auspicious eyes, the two eyebrows should be contracted; the gaze should be directed upward, and both eye-lids should be slightly closed. (133)
O Leader of the Gods, the trident situated in the sky should be visualized;
then, with both hands, one should perform the pressing of that which has entered through the side door.
But it moves swiftly upward to where the lotus-born aperture is; thus one remains established in the channels, O leader of heroes, and not otherwise. (135)
When one has become established in the state of the *nāḍīs*, then one should abandon the causal state through *recaka*,
*pūraka*, and *kumbhaka* yogas, along with their supporting practices.
Thus, when one has abandoned the causal [state] and becomes equal to Śakti, then the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇiman* shall belong to him. || 137 ||
One perceives the objects of the past, the future, and likewise the present; there is no doubt in this matter: Maheśvara has the channels as his support. || 138 ||
When the lunar power (śakti-soma) becomes present in the navel as the past, in the heart as the present, and in the uvula (lambaka) as the future; || 139 ||

O Goddess, one who has arisen through wisdom (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*) should enter the eternal body; it is said to be situated in the *nāda*, and previously indeed situated in the *bindu*. 140.
Now listen, O Great Goddess, to how the state of being established in the spies occurs, and hear their classification so that it may be known according to reality. || 141 ||
The movement of thirty-six finger-breadths, from the heart-lotus down to that state,
occurs by means of the sixteen-fold division through the sequential application of the *tuṭi*s and so forth.
Indeed, it must be characterized by time, for the day may come to an end; O beloved, this very form of calculation is determined by time.
One should utter *sauṃ* with division from one place to another, according to the determination of the doubt regarding the pairs of the unawakened and the awakened. 144.
He abandons the first part as it reaches from the heart-lotus upward;
the second [part] is at the tip of the nose, and the third is joined with the Śakti.
One who remains there may turn back as long as one does not find reality; but once the supreme peace is known, even while remaining there, one is no longer afflicted.
When the ignorant one goes downward to the base of the power (śakti), he is then said to be "asleep"; when he rises again from the heart, he is called "awakening."

Having attained power, the wise one is to be known as awakened; he awakens within the portion of the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī). Then he becomes transcendent and perfectly awakened, and the state of Unmanā arises. || 148 ||
Neither time, nor the movement of the digits, nor reality, nor cause—[this is] the supreme, pure, perfect nirvāṇa, arrived at through the lineage of the gurus. (149)
Having known that, one is liberated; having gone [there], one is not born again. I shall explain to you how the six paths—the hexad of paths—reside within the vital breath (prāṇa). || 150 ||

That which is consciousness and perception from the feet up to the top of the head is to be known as the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), and likewise the path of the principles (tattvādhvan). || 151 ||
The vital breath (prāṇa), whose continuum is composed of the digits (kalās), always moves;
Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā are proclaimed to be in the lower portion. || 152 ||
Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Ūrdhvaśānta are established;
beyond that is the supreme state, the imperishable plane above it. (153)

In this way, the digits of the point (bindu-kalā) are to be known, as well as those consisting of the power of resonance (nāda-śakti), and the digits of the pervasive one (vyāpinī), according to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader. || 154 ||
All these are established in the vital breath (prāṇa), and their dissolution is said to occur at the end of the breath.
Thus has the path of the parts (kalādhvan) been described; now learn the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan). || 155 ||
All phonemes, whose nature is sound, exist within this world of the moving and the unmoving, established through fifty divisions across infinite millions of scriptures. (156)
Sound is declared to be the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, the phonemes arise from the vital breath. Where sound goes to its dissolution, there they too go to their dissolution. || 157 ||
O lady of excellent hips, transcending sound, he is united with reality;
O Goddess, he is liberated, omnipresent, and devoid of both merit and demerit. || 158 ||
When one has reached the Śiva-principle, one no longer looks downward;
however, by means of unrighteousness one goes downward, whereas by means of righteousness one may go upward once again.
Having abandoned duality through consciousness, one becomes all-pervading here;
the path of phonemes has been fully explained, and now the path of words is described here. (160)
Those eighty-one words which are established in the King of Vidyās—those words consist of phonemes, and those phonemes are traditionally held to consist of vital breaths. || 161 ||
Therefore, all these stages (padas) are established according to the sequence of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus has the path of the stages (padādhvan) been explained; now learn from me the path of mantra (mantrādhvan).
The elevenfold mantra is established by means of Śakti;
it moves perpetually within the vital breath (prāṇa) up to the end of the eleventh principle (tattva). || 163 ||
The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the Bindu;
the Half-moon, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, and the end of the Nāda (Nādānta). || 164 ||
Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā are remembered as the eleventh;
Unmanā is beyond that, and what is beyond that is the stainless (nirāmaya). || 165 ||
The mantras likewise abide thus in the vital breath (prāṇa); now the utterance by means of power (śakti) is described.
The letter *ha* is traditionally held to be the vital breath, well-functioning and having the form of a plow (*halākṛti*).
The letter *a* is joined with the head, the letter *u* with the feet, and the letter *m* with the measure (*mātrā*);
thus the pronunciation of the syllable becomes distinct.
Through the union with the Bindu at the head, one attains a beautiful voice; Nāda is said to be his mouth, for he utters sound as Nāda.
By this very yoga, that Self is called the Puruṣa;
it moves through all living beings by way of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa. || 169 ||
It dissolves into the principle of Śakti; by means of higher knowledge, one proceeds upward.
Having transcended Vyāpinī and Samanā, one reaches Śiva in Unmanā. || 170 ||
The power residing within the Śiva-principle does not move; it becomes all-pervading.
This is declared to be the utterance of power (śaktyuccāra); the abandonment of causes is now described.
The letter *ha* is the essence of the power of vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*), and the letter *a* denotes Brahman;
its renunciation occurs within the heart, and the letter *u* denotes Viṣṇu. (172)
The letter *ma*, which denotes Rudra, shall be abandoned at the throat;
he too abandons it in the middle of the palate, and the *bindu* itself is Īśvara. (173)
Sadāśiva, who is expressed by the *nāda*, performs the emission (*tyāga*) of that [seed-syllable] between the eyebrows;
the emission of that is prescribed from the forehead up to the crown of the head.
But Śakti is all-pervasive and samanā; among these, Śiva is to be expressed as their referent.
One should abandon Śakti at the crown and in the center, and above that, one should abandon Vyāpinī.
Having abandoned the state of *samanā* and *unmanā*, dissolution (*laya*) is then said to occur;
O Dear One, one should likewise abandon [all states] through increasingly subtle and most subtle dispositions.
Bestowing various fruits of accomplishment through entities that are gross and increasingly grosser,
he is established as non-existence, the subtle, the ultimate, and the supreme state.

The state of *unmanā* is the supreme condition; the gross [state] is considered superior to that, while the void (*śūnya*) is further beyond it, and the touchless (*asparśa*) is likewise even higher than that. (178)
Sound, light, as well as mantras, the causes, and the worlds—the worlds consisting of the five elements—are presided over by the causes. || 179 ||
He who meditates upon the worlds according to their single form that is about to be described attains the state of Lord of the Worlds; he should meditate on Śiva as being identical with that.
In the practice of the causes beginning with Brahmā, one should contemplate their embodied forms;
by doing so, one attains identity with that which possesses the characteristics previously described.
Through mantras, one attains the perfection of mantra by means of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship;
through meditation on the previously described form, it is perfected—of this there is no doubt. (182)
Through meditation on the light, the lord of yogis shall attain the perfection of yoga;
when he reaches identification with that [light], he becomes the sovereign of yogis. (183)
Through meditation on sound, one becomes the essence of sound and the fulfiller of all speech;
through meditation on touch, one becomes the essence of touch and the cause of the world. || 184 ||

Through meditation on emptiness, the self becomes empty, pervasive, and all-pervading; by means of the yoga of meditative concentration on the equal breath, the yogi shall attain omniscience. || 185 ||
One should always contemplate that supreme, subtle state beyond the mind, which is non-existence; it is called the state that transcends all senses and is imperceptible. (186)
By making existence free from affliction through the state of the existence of non-existence,
one attains the state of non-existence which is liberated from all limiting conditions.
This is for you the explanation of the abandonment of causes and the abandonment of time;
the vital breath (prāṇa) is declared to consist of the number sixteen tuṭis. (188)
Relying upon two *tuṭis*, each one is known as a Bhairava;
they proceed in this manner through the division of day and night, O fair-faced one. (189)
They say that the ninth supreme deity arises from his splendor;
I shall likewise tell you how one should abandon [the breath] within the vital breath at all times.
The sixteen *tuṭis* are the constituent parts (*karaṇas*) of time, by means of which all that consists of speech proceeds when the times are well-established. (191)
The tuṭi, lava, nimeṣa, kāṣṭhā, and likewise the kalā;
the muhūrta, day and night, the fortnight, the month, and likewise the season. || 192 ||
The half-year, the year, the yuga, the manvantara,
as well as the kalpa and the mahākalpa— these he should abandon at the end of his power.
In the aspect of the all-pervading, there is a supreme time; one should abandon that as its constituent part.
That seventeenth [aspect] is to be known as the "supreme half" (parārdha) situated beyond.
And that eighteenth time he should abandon at the end of the Samanā;
but the Supreme, the Imperishable, pervades all time within time. || 195 ||
Others should be employed with disregard; in that state, time does not exist.
It is eternal, eternally risen, and all-pervading; one should not abandon it in the form of Nāda.
And that which is eternally arisen is to be attained; one is born always equal to it. Thus there is the relinquishing of time, which is then called the state of emptiness.
The upper void, the lower void, and the middle void as the third—
one should rely upon these three voids from above, below, and in the middle. Furthermore,
the fourth is the pervasive void (*vyāpinī-śūnya*), and *samanā* is the fifth here.
Likewise, the sixth [is] for the *unmanī*; these six are established as the *sāmaya* [levels].
All of them, when presided over by reality (*tattva*), grant results even as *sāmaya*.
Having abandoned those six voids, effect dissolution in the seventh.
That emptiness is supreme and subtle, devoid of all states;
it is called "non-empty" and "empty," and emptiness is said to be non-existence.
Non-existence is designated as that wherein all entities have come to an end.
That supreme, peaceful state of pure existence—how and in what manner does it abide?
Wherever there is no sound, even where gross things are established, there the supreme void abides, pervading everything. (202–203)
Pervading all gross objects, it becomes gross through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
thus, by means of the distinction between the subtle and the gross, it is established in this manner.
Having attained that [state], one becomes equal to it—of this there is no doubt.
The doctrine of emptiness has been fully explained for your pleasure, O Goddess worshipped by the gods.
Now listen to how it is established within Śakti,
and how, O sinless one, she exists through the union with the colorless and the colored.
Thus I shall speak with certainty, O fair-eyed one:
those mantras which were previously spoken in an innumerable number of seventy million,
though hidden in the past, O Goddess, have now been brought down in the form of letters.

Therefore, those mantras do not succeed even if recited hundreds of millions of times. O lady of excellent hips, that imperishable power which is said to be the very life-force of mantras— devoid of it, they are as fruitless as autumn clouds.
O blessed lady, this has been concealed from the gods, the ṛṣis, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
from the siddhas, the hosts of nāgas, and these human yogins.
Indeed, it is hidden from those lowest of men who are devoid of devotion.
They do not recognize the Guru as a god, nor likewise the commitments (samaya) declared in the scriptures;
devoted to hypocrisy and crookedness, they are devoid of ritual action for the sake of their own greed.
For this reason, my power (vīrya) has been concealed by me.
O Lord of Gods, when that [Mātṛkā] is concealed, the remaining phonemes are merely isolated.
O Goddess, that Mātṛkā which is supreme and endowed with splendor—
by her the entire universe is pervaded, reaching as far as the world of Brahmā.
But when, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, that which resides therein exists as all-pervading—
just as the Lord, though established in no letter, is established in all letters and is omnipresent—
I shall explain that to you for the sake of definitive certainty, O you who are honored by the gods.
That power which is supreme, subtle, and proclaimed as being beyond conventional conduct,
having coiled around the *bindu* in the heart, is like a sleeping serpent;
O highly fortunate Umā, while sleeping there, it perceives nothing at all.
Having cast the fourteen worlds, along with the moon, fire, sun, and stars,
into her belly, that goddess fell into a state of unconsciousness;
she was awakened by a supreme sound consisting of pure knowledge.

O lady of excellent complexion, as long as the churning by the drop residing within the belly continues with the force of whirling, so long does the churning persist within the form of the Śakti. But when the first division has arisen, the drop indeed possesses the luster of splendor.
By churning that drop, the subtle *kalā* Kuṇḍalinī [is revealed].
The Lord Bindu, consisting of four *kalās*, having entered the belly of Śakti,
arises before one through the yoga of the churned and the churning by means of straightening.
That supreme power is known as Jyeṣṭhā, situated between two points (bindus).
When she is stirred by the point, she becomes the line known as Amṛtakuṇḍalī;
she should be understood as Rekhinī when situated between both points.
She is proclaimed as the threefold path and is sung of by the name Raudrī.
She is designated as the Obstructress (Nirodhī), who blocks the way to liberation;
she has the form of a crescent of the moon and is Ambikā, the Half-Moonlight.
The one supreme Śakti indeed arises in three ways;
from these, when combined and separated, she is born as the ninefold group.
She is remembered as ninefold, characterized by the nine groups.

O Goddess, leader of the gods, she who resides in the five mantras according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta is declared to be fivefold; she should be known thus. O Goddess, she who dwells in the twelve vowels is proclaimed to have twelve stations.
The letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa* abide in fifty distinct divisions.
That which consists of a single *aṇu* is situated in the region of the heart; that which consists of two *aṇus* is to be known as being in the throat;
and that which consists of three *aṇus* is to be understood as being situated at the root of the tongue.
The manifestation of the phonemes occurs at the tip of the tongue; of this there is no doubt.
In this way, the manifestation of sound occurs, and the moving and unmoving world is pervaded by sound.
One should first place Raudrī on the head, and Vāmā is proclaimed to be in the mouth.
Ambikā is said to be the arm, and Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as the weapon.
Śrīkaṇṭha is indeed declared to be the all-pervading Supreme Lord.
Just as there is one, so too are all sixteen great winds.
After that, twenty-five [are taught], and above those, nine are traditionally recorded.
By this sequential method, the emergence of the fifty [phonemes] has been declared by the God of Gods according to the distinction between cause and effect.
Thus, O Pārvatī, the individual extraction of the twelve thousand names of the host of Rudras has been proclaimed here;
these too are all-pervasive, eternal, consisting of sound, and endowed with qualities.
This distinction between the signified and the signifier, which stands beyond the nine [newly created beings],
was established by me, the Creator, for the sake of worldly transaction through the analysis of words.
Yet, there is no word without the Rudras, nor is there any meaning, nor indeed is there any comprehension without them.
The body is brilliantly illuminated by the fifty-fold masses of sounds;
through the meditation on the five-crested Rudra, the Mātṛkā is attained here.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should know that everything originates from that Mātṛkā.
There is no designation superior to the Mātṛkā, nor is there any mantra higher than the Mātṛkā.
Through the division of gross and subtle, the body arises from the Mātṛkā;
wherever sound is produced, there it also goes to its dissolution.
Just as a drop arises and perishes in the midst of water,
even so the essence of sound dissolves from the *manobindu*.
Having abandoned Raudrī at the head, one should raise up Jyeṣṭhā as a weapon.
Ambikā, having abandoned her face, is situated in the region of the arms;
she alone is to be known as Kuṇḍalī, and nothing else is perceived.
In this way, indeed, both destruction and likewise origination come to be.
O fair-faced one, he who understands both arising and destruction shall become a powerful hero, just as you, my beloved;
he shall become a lord of practitioners, worthy of worship, and the most venerable of all.
O auspicious lady, Vāmā is remembered as Brahmā; Jyeṣṭhā is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu.
O beautiful woman, Raudrī is Rudra, and they know Ambikā to be Īśvara.
Śiva, however, is the union whose form is sound, the supreme one consisting of Nāda.
O Goddess, five causal agents are established in their pervasiveness;
likewise, the powers (śaktis) are seen in every phoneme.
Icchā is declared to be Raudrī, and Jñānā is proclaimed to be Vāmā.
O lady of auspicious gaze, Kriyā is declared to be Jyeṣṭhā; she should be known as the Mother.
Sunrise is to be known through Vāmā, while Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as midday.
Sandhyā is to be understood as Raudrī, and at that very time, sunset occurs.
Recaka is said to be through Vāmā; the wise know pūraka to be through Jyeṣṭhā;
kumbhaka is to be known as being through Raudrī, while Ambikā resides in the state of natural composure.
Iḍā is declared to be Vāmā, Raudrī is known as Piṅgalā,
and Suṣumṇā, who resides in Jyeṣṭhā, is said to be the Śakti of Viṣṇu.
Kuṇḍalī is to be known at the time of manifestation; she is proclaimed as Vāmā.
Jyeṣṭhā resides in separation, and Raudrī is said to be in dissolution. (251)
O Leader of the Gods, the Mother should likewise be known as transcending the elements;
she is to be known as Kuṇḍalī, situated at the navel, with the form of a sleeping serpent. (252)
Above the location of the throat is Raudrī, where Rudra, the Lord of the World, resides;
Jyeṣṭhā is in the flow at the center, situated between the two points (bindus).
Ambikā, residing in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), is to be known by the knower of reality;
Kuṇḍalinī is to be understood as Śamanā, and she is proclaimed to be the waking state (jāgrat). || 254 ||
Jyeṣṭhā, who has entered into sleep, is indeed Raudrī, the bringer of the Unmanā state;
O Goddess, that state known as deep sleep is called Unmanā.
Ambikā is beyond the Unmanā state, abiding in the station of Turya, and is auspicious;
she is to be known as the first Kuṇḍalinī, while the second is Manonmanī.
The third, however, is named Bindu; the universe is permeated by the three powers. It is the third [power] that presides over manifestation, separation, and dissolution. (257)
Beyond the state of dissolution, supreme, peaceful, all-pervading, the Supreme Lord, free from action and cause, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted. || 258 ||
And having known this, O lady of excellent hips, one shall not undergo birth again;
the seizing of that which resides within the *kuṇḍalinī* must be understood by the wise. (259)
Just as a bird perched in the sky sees its prey, O beloved, and swiftly draws it toward itself with great speed; || 260 ||
In that very same way, the lord of yogis should draw back the mind-bindu;
just as an arrow situated within a reed, when struck by a machine, flies forth. || 261 ||
Likewise, O lady of excellent hips, the drop (bindu) runs by means of upward movement;
having made the void the instrument, one should join the mouth of the void to the head of the void.
The tortoise, ending with a vowel and joined with two consonants, should be applied to Maṅgala;
its impulsion is by means of the udāna breath until it reaches the opening of that void.
When the auspicious [mark] is joined with the tortoise and purified by the arrow-weapon itself, O fair-faced one, the path of the twice-born is undoubtedly purified. 264.
One should observe the grasping precisely through the pure path;
the grasping must be performed by the mind of that which has entered the support of power (śakti). 265.
But there may be a sign for that grasping, O fair-faced one:
a trembling located at the navel is to be known, as well as yawning and a distracted face. (266)
The falling of tears, the knitting of the eyebrows, and likewise mental agitation—these are the signs when [the breath] is at the navel;
now hear those pertaining to the throat.
With the mantra situated at the throat, one shakes the limbs and emits sounds in many ways;
there is shaking of the head, incoherent speech, and the great sound of the syllable *hūṃ*. || 268 ||
But when he has passed beyond that, O excellent Ambikā, into the abode of Rudra, then his signs of attainment will appear; listen to them with a concentrated mind.
Abiding in Rudra, the practitioner perceives the scriptures, mudrās, and mantras in manifold ways;
he causes even those scriptures not previously heard to resound.
Above that, O Great Goddess, is the state known as Visarga;
when one is established in Visarga, O Goddess, then one hears the Sound.
And upon contact, one perceives it as cool, like the peaks of the Himalayas;
then, O Goddess, that station of power attains oneness with the Sādākhya.
O fair-faced one, the state of being beyond the mind (unmanatva) is indeed the station of power regarding the sense objects;
here, the attainment of the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) occurs, without a doubt. (273)
O beautiful one, if the dissolution (laya) becomes firmly established right there, then one rises up quickly; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
That which resides in the apertures is to be known as all-pervading, yet that which transcends it is all-encompassing;
just as space within a jar exists as if delimited.
In this way, O Goddess, although omnipresence appears to be severed from the body, it nevertheless returns to a state of oneness when the jar is broken, just as [the space within] does. || 276 ||
Just as the single existence of both the external and the internal shines forth,
so too does the elemental self shine forth, liberated from its bonds.
Just as a lamp situated within a jar illuminates only one part,
so too the self, residing within the subtle body (liṅga), is refined by the activity of the mind.
By those who, without knowing the supreme reality, have merely imagined Śiva-hood as being a residual state of bondage devoid of all temporal adjuncts; (281)
And those worshippers of the self in the Śaiva tradition do not go to the state of Śiva;
rather, being colored by the self-nature of the self, they attain the realization of the principle of the self. || 282 ||
Those who worship deities by conceptualizing them as having forms obtain a basis for those [conceptions], but they are not liberated in the ultimate sense. || 283 ||
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should worship that which abides in its own nature (svabhāva).
Listen now as to how that which abides in its own nature is further described. || 284 ||
There is no cessation, nor rising, nor measurement, nor conjunction;
having known that which abides in its own nature, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (285)
Volition is indeed the great bond, the cause of becoming that must be severed;
by abandoning it, the yogi is liberated, for one who possesses volitional constructs remains bound. (286)
There is no mind, nor is there anything to be thought, nor is a thinker perceived; as long as one conceptualizes the deity, for that long bondage continues. 287.
There is neither the *bindu*, nor the *nāda*, nor the movement belonging to the six paths;
it does not exist on the path of the utterance of *śakti*, nor at the time of the abandonment of the causes.
It is neither the state of emptiness nor non-existence, nor power, nor even Śiva;
for this is the latent impression of ignorance that binds one with the fear of saṃsāra. 289.
Generally, no one will find contentment in that which does not exist;
therefore, having abandoned that, one must relinquish all the snares of hope without exception. (290)
Hope alone is the great bond by which the entire world is pervaded;
as long as it is not abandoned, true power indeed does not exist.
That is the ochre robe of those who proclaim liberation, wherein everything has come to an end;
he who feels no longing even for liberation attains liberation. (292)
There is no abiding in existence for liberation, nor is there giving, nor conceptualization;
that which is a false view in every respect—that, for those who speak of liberation, is liberation. (293)
Liberation is that which is inexpressible, beyond the conceptualization of affirmation and negation; it arises from knowledge, while ignorance is to be abandoned. (294)
The entire world has that as its form, yet nothing has that as its form;
therefore, the wise should here abide in the nature of formlessness. (295)
That creation which proceeds from the state of reality is called the "elemental" (bhūta);
it is the blissful form of Brahman, and one who knows it never fears anything. || 296 ||
Having realized that everything indeed consists of the Self, there is nothing whatsoever to be done;
if there is the notion of existence, then there is bondage, without a doubt. (297)
Just as a silkworm binds itself by its own self through its own efforts with various kinds of cocoons, so too, O Bhāva, does one bind oneself. || 298 ||
He who is bound shall be liberated; for what liberation is there for one who is not bound?
The bonds are both innate and adventitious, and they are based upon the state of duality. (299)
O beloved, whatever is mental in nature, characterized by the volitions of the mind, is here imagined by itself; having abandoned that which is mental, one should abandon whatever consists of speech.
Everything consists of existence and non-existence; the mind is characterized by volitional construction. Wherever the mind operates among pure and impure entities, [therein it is bound]. (301)
For one in whom equanimity arises toward the conceptual distinctions of caste and non-caste, as well as toward what is edible and inedible, for him nothing at all has been born.
One should first abandon all existent things, and then become established in non-existence; having abandoned even that non-existence, one will abide in the state of intrinsic nature.
Just as water resting on a rock, when evaporated by the rays of the sun, is neither drunk by anyone nor does it remain in that very place; || 304 ||
The mind of one who knows reality likewise attains a state beyond logical proof; like the all-pervading wind, it carries away the earth, the sky, and all else by its power. || 305 ||
Just as a mountain of trees, being struck with a great force and bursting apart, goes to utter destruction in that very instant, so too does the mind of one who possesses knowledge.
Just as clouds, having spread across the sky, vanish into destruction in that very instant, so too does the mind of the wise man. 307.
Just as the rain from a cloud causes the lowlands and highlands, the waters and dry lands of a region to vanish in that very instant, so too does the state of being without a home [vanish].
Just as the flame of a fire, through contact with fuel, reaches a state beyond comparison and perishes in that very instant, so do the wise know the mind to be empty. 309.
Just as the sound of a conch shell, O Goddess, is heard with a vast resonance and then at that very moment subsides, so do the wise know the mind in the state of equilibrium.
Then, relying on dispassion, one should exhaust that [karmic] thread for the sake of liberation through difficult penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, just as salt dissolves in the Unmanā state.
Among those many who have grasped at detachment and thereby exhausted themselves, not even one has reached here without logical justification. (312)
Celibacy, dedication to austerity, purity, and other such restraints—liberation is not accomplished by these; rather, it is internal disposition alone that is the cause in this matter. || 313 ||
The fire, the darbha grass, the mantras, the hotṛ priest, that which is to be offered, the praṇītā water, the sacrificial seats, and the arrangement of the initiation and the sacrifice. || 314 ||
This aggregate of volitions is the cause of your awakening; it is non-dual, free from conceptual construction, devoid of sense organs, and without defining characteristics.
How can there be a mark for that which is markless? How can there be a mind for that which is mindless? The wise should constantly establish themselves in the state beyond the mind. (316)
Non-existence persists eternally, while existence must be abandoned; for one who has become non-existent, that state is "it does not exist."

There is no liberation, for there is a great bondage; one should contemplate everything as indeed empty. The consciousness of a moving or unmoving self exists only in dependence upon the fluctuations of the mind. || 318 ||
How could it be made motionless within the body by anyone, as long as one contemplates knowledge alone, which is the support of higher realization? 319.

When [the mind] is agitated by the vital breath (vāyu), ignorance (avidyā) arises; however, the mind is thoroughly conquered by the steadfast through practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 320 ||

At any other time, one should perform that which was previously conquered [by the senses], for it would be fruitless; therefore, having understood this, one should regard the objects of the senses as both moving and unmoving.
Like a jar, its form is fragile and like the flash of lightning; having abandoned all [worldly things] for the sake of liberation, fix your mind on the nihilist (nāstika). 322.
The Goddess said:
O God, O Great Lord, a great curiosity has arisen within me: since that which is not there cannot be perceived, how can there be any movement for that which is unperceivable?
Meditation, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and various forms of contemplative cultivation—for what purpose were these taught by you, O God, O Supreme Lord? (324)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Various forms, colors, and diverse hundreds of thousands [of signs]—all this has been revealed for the purpose of purifying the mind. (325)
For the mind is ever restless, without support, and beyond the senses; how can it be restrained, its movement being swifter than the wind? (326)
As long as one meditates on one [object], another arises; thus, neither meditation nor the focal point will ever be accomplished. (327)
For this reason, everything arising from the mind—whether it be a target, meditation, or that which consists of conceptual construction—must be abandoned entirely without remainder.
Having abandoned the sense of "mine" everywhere, one should contemplate, "I am not. Delighting in the practice of non-duality, one realizes: "I am not, nor does another exist. (329)
For as long as one does not find it in this way, so long nothing belongs to him; however, that object which is the "I" is bound within the three qualities (guṇas).
O Goddess, as long as he does not abandon desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, dispassion, or likewise knowledge, he will remain obstructed. (331)
As long as one is not liberated by these means, from where could there be any [higher] destination for them? For one whose pleasure and pain are equal, there is neither going nor coming. || 332 ||
Just as a calf turns away from its mother’s udder when the milk has been exhausted, so too, upon the exhaustion of passion, Nirvana is the supreme state for men.
This entire world is attached to children, wife, and family; having abandoned that and become free from the qualities (nirguṇa), one attains nirvāṇa.
Even those who have reached the peak of existence (bhavāgra), being intent on and devoted to that yoga, fall back into the ocean of worldly existence when dragged by the goad of egoism.
Having abandoned the sense of "I," one should abandon the sense of "mine"; having relinquished hope entirely, one who is free from desire is highly praised. (336)
"Even a twice-born man who is a killer of a fetus or one who violates the teacher's bed, if he possesses knowledge of the four Vedas, shall behold equality"—thus another Śruti has declared. (337)
The liberated one, whose self is liberated, perceives only the Self everywhere; for one who beholds this oneness, there is neither "I" nor "another. (338)
He who perceives through reality the oneness existing in many states, like a single thread of wool divided a thousandfold, stands established in the essence of aesthetic unity (sāmarasya). || 339 ||
Equanimity toward all beings, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal—by that he attains equality with them; he is called one who is free from transformation.
He whose movement is the course of intrinsic nature, who is the Lord of the imperishability of intrinsic nature—for him whose name is "Great Renown," no conceptual construction is taught. 341.
"He by whom this world is pervaded is to be known as Hiraṇyagarbha. The Goddess said:
It is completely liberated from all entities and devoid of all gender markers.
"In non-duality there is no second; how can it remain unmoving? Bhairava said:
O beautiful one, when it shall abide in its own nature by means of its own nature, [then it will be liberated]. || 343 ||
His [knowledge] becomes immovable and is never moved; yet, the self-knowledge appears to move in relation to the fluctuations of the mind. (344)
That by which all this is filled is worshipped by yogins; it is constantly practiced through austerities and sacrificed to with sacrifices.
This very Self is "not this, not this" (neti neti), for it is not born; it does not decay, for it cannot decay. Therefore, this has been declared thus.
But attachment, O Goddess, to these very subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell is known to be the cause of the arising of saṃsāra. (347)
From attachment desire arises; from desire comes the grasping for possessions;
and from grasping comes distress. Therefore, one should abandon attachment.
Having abandoned attachment to the world and likewise attachment to the scriptures, one who is completely liberated from all attachments goes to the imperishable state.

It is non-existence beyond all cultivation, devoid of both the object of awakening and the awakener; it is indeed transcendent through its very being, having as its sphere that which is beyond conceptual proliferation.
O Goddess, he for whom this [reality] remains—free from action and cause, and devoid of logical reasoning—attains the supreme state. 351.
O lady of excellent limbs, once one has gone there, one never goes downward again. O Goddess, this is the reality considered by me to be the supreme, partless (niṣkala) state. 352.
Nothing superior to him exists in the three worlds—he whose mind is ever undeluded regarding the world as being the self of all beings. (353)
And its being composed of that alone is the truth, the absolute truth; there is no doubt. The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Gods, [this applies] to the left and right paths as well as to the Siddhānta.
It is proclaimed to be threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme—and is endowed with meditation and concentration, as well as joined with yoga, mantra, and ritual action. || 355 ||
For them, there shall be accomplishment and liberation, but never for others; nor can there be birth where there is no abiding in any way whatsoever. (356)
"Truly, truly, and again truly, you have performed the withdrawal of the ocean of the world consisting of speech in every tantra. (357)
"O Mahādeva, there is no truth in that which has been spoken by you. Bhairava said:
Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yoginīs, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas; || 358 ||
Among them, you said, "O my beloved, there is no truth for me"; today I have understood that your mind is difficult to propitiate.
"You think it has already been told, yet you ask again and again; nevertheless, I shall speak further—listen with certainty, my dear. (360)
Just as you have conceived the convention, so shall I explain to you that which is the supreme reality—tranquil, inconceivable, and free from all support.
I have described that reality according to its gross, subtle, and supreme aspects; that reality is the causeless source of all things. (362)

If it is argued that this is illogical, [we reply: here, origination consists of those qualities; like a piece of wood, that supreme deity and likewise the self are of the nature of dissolution. (363)

If both are equally common [to all], who here in this cycle of existence is the master? How could there be an origination from that which is with impurity, and likewise from a self that is with impurity? (364)
The view that [the soul] is not the master by its own nature is considered an external position; it concerns a subject that is liberated from the *puryaṣṭaka* and transcends all causes.

Because it is distinct from the relationship between the signified and the signifier, because it is without any trace [of conceptualization], because it is devoid of all phenomenal proliferation, and because its sphere transcends the senses. || 366 ||
It is understood that the emergence of another reality arises from its own inherent nature, just as rice sprouts arise from rice, and kodrava sprouts from kodrava.
The arising of the Supreme Self from another reality is not possible; for how could there be a seedless birth, like that of a seed, which is of the nature of both being and non-being? (368)
Endowed with the four qualities, yet having as its sphere that which transcends those qualities; for the Self is indeed without beginning or end, and karma is likewise held to be beginningless.
If [the cause] consists of power (śakti) and the five elements, what is produced here? Since their production is mutually dependent, how could it attain permanence? || 370 ||
Because it is not established beyond that point, it is held to be impermanent; the connection with various classes of beings proceeds from its manifold elaboration.

How is it that even though he is free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca), he is still understood by those who see reality? He is inconceivable, immeasurable, devoid of thought, and likewise supreme. (372)
How can one whose self has abandoned all defects be an awakened Buddha and an awakener? Sound is the quality of space; hearing is its perceiver. (373)

In that very way, how could the bliss of the object of perception arise from the supreme reality? For the self is ignorant, impermanent, and a bound soul (paśu), while Śiva is something else, within the scope of recollection.
And how is it known that he is without means and stainless? If scripture were the means, then there would be a contradiction regarding the state of being without means. (375)
And how can the Lord, whose sphere transcends the path of speech, be reached through a means? For the means is the Samanā, which is designated as the mind and the senses. || 376 ||
How can transcendence of the senses be possible for that Lord, who is perceivable by the organs of sense, gross, and subject to destruction? (377)
How can that which is subject to destruction be the divine Supreme Self? If consciousness exists in the supreme reality, then that consciousness must be conceptual. (378)
How could there be an entry of conceptualization into the non-conceptual? For the Buddha, the Jina, Śiva, Ātman, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are merely designations.
But how could one who is ignorant regarding the name be ignorant regarding the object of worship? One who is rendered unconscious by poison likewise becomes free from conceptual construction. (380)
For those who are deeply asleep while dwelling in the womb and for those dying at the feet [of the Lord], liberation occurs first; for others, however, there is doubt.
Who knows whether there is or is not the destruction of conceptual construction? Why, how, when, whose, by what, who, and where is it established? (382)
Thus, it is not possible to say that the hare's horn alone does not exist; for elsewhere, both the horn and the hare are seen to exist separately. (383)
There is no connection at all with a horn because it does not exist on the head of a rabbit; furthermore, there is a mutual incompatibility between the sense faculties and the mind. 384.
A relationship with the Supreme Self has never been observed anywhere at any time; it is difficult to discern, for if it were ever known at the very beginning, [it would have remained so]. (385)
Because it is mobile, the mind is not stable; how, then, could liberation exist therein? Knowledge, the vehicle, and likewise the immediate—these three are held to be the body. (386)
The entire world is born from the knowledge of the Omniscient One; it is beyond the senses, inconceivable, and characterized by a nature free from conceptual proliferation.
The body of Lord Śiva is held to be extremely subtle and consisting of pure knowledge; whereas that which is non-self has taken on a physical form, being powerful and pleasing to behold. || 388 ||
Having manifested his own nature, he goes to that state by his own will; in one moment that form is seen, and in another moment it dissolves into gnosis. 389.
Because it brings about what is desired by its very nature, it is proclaimed as "immediate" (sadyas); even after cutting through or piercing to the roots [of past karma], no fruit is seen there.
That [effect] is seen to arise suddenly from the desire of another; from a seed comes a tree, and from that tree [comes] a seed—thus they are produced from one another. (391)
And arising by its very nature is essentially without beginning or end; it is like the demonstration of bees [attracted] to the end of the fruit of a mango tree. (392)
The *āmalaka* fruit does not have a lineage of seeds in other trees; for its production is seen to arise from the earth, water, and likewise from space, despite their mutual opposition. (393)
Even here, the fact that things arise determinately would establish their birth from the void; for it is not possible for them to exist in a manner contrary to their own respective natures. (394)

And having brought this about by himself, Bhuvaneśa established a rule: "He who, knowing [the truth], is free from objects and free from conceptual construction, is [liberated] even while possessing a body. (395)

How can one who is unconscious and ignorant be liberated? Such a person wanders through saṃsāra; the conceptualization of dwelling in the worldly cycle of the household is itself characterized by conceptual construction.
The householder arises as the Self, and immediately following that is the family-man;
therein lies the dissolution of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness.
That reality is the abode of all accomplishments, imperishable, free from attachment to mental cultivation, and the bringer about of the cessation of saṃsāra. || 398 ||
That state into which existence dissolves by its own nature is the [Supreme] State; egoity dissolves into the intellect, the intellect into the mind, and that mind [dissolves] into [the Unmanifest].
As long as the mind dissolves into the mind, so long is that the supreme state;
the sacrifice of the sun is transmigratory existence, and the sacrifice of the moon is likewise the other.
Since both of these have receded into the ocean of consciousness, those who perceive reality consider that there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. (401)
How is it that their mind, having moved swiftly, reaches that state, whereas the wind, though moving, does not reach the released space? || 402 ||
In the same way, the mind of yogins does not reach reality once it is liberated;
the mind wavers, but the self does not, and therefore there is no wavering of it.
Upon its destruction, how indeed can the self, which was moving, become immovable?
Men devoted to the yoga of action are deceived by their own minds. (404)
Through the application of the yoga of non-conceptualization, they are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Knowledge directed toward the focal object becomes a state of fixed meaning. (405)

But that thorough knowledge of the ultimate reality, which is established upon all objects of perception and bestows everything through its discernment, belongs to those whose minds are no longer attached to grasping. 406.
The knowledge pertaining to an objective referent is said to belong to the ignorant;
it persists until the destruction of that referent, which occurs after a further period of time. (407)
For the discerning one, knowledge becomes the perfect ground for all accomplishments;
it is the thorough realization of the ultimate truth for one whose mind delights in grasping.
In the ultimate sense, those yogins are declared to be omniscient; that state in which no connection [between object and cognition] is perceived is remembered as the supreme. (409)
Although liberation here consists precisely of such a connection with another, that connection is of the nature of pleasure and pain, arising from the substance and the sense organs. || 410 ||
Because of the presence of impurities (kaṣāya), transmigratory existence occurs; he who has abandoned these two is liberated.
Even if stainless, one who is attached to dissolution is considered to be with dissolution and thus possessed of impurity.
The self transmigrates when it is unwell; when it is well, it is proclaimed to be liberated.
Furthermore, cognition that has a cause is impermanent because it is sublated by something else. (412)
That consciousness which is signless and eternal is indeed liberation;
that knowledge, that supreme state, that is liberation, and that is union.
This knowledge is signless (nirnimitta), and from it everything proceeds;
its very signlessness is the cause of the proceeding of creation. ||414||
For cessation is not always experienced through direct perception;
if reality were something determined by the sense faculties, it would [be so perceived]. (415)
Were all those who were then taught by another teacher not to have become knowers of reality, if that which is perceived by the senses were not reality? (416)
What further proof can be stated for its existence?
That which is gross and determined by the eyes and other senses is perishable. (417)
How can one become a knower of reality merely by cognizing that? [For] what is the ultimate limit of the gross, and what is the ultimate limit of liberation? (418)
Not even the slightest subtle difference exists between those two;
likewise, one who is blind does not see forms, nor does one whose mind is elsewhere.
Because that which is to be remembered is not subject to deviation, even the aggregate does not exist;
therefore, the eye does not see form, nor does the mind as an aggregate.
For this is the supreme secret into which the world does not penetrate; nothing whatsoever is added to it, nor is there anything else beyond this. 421.
But one who perceives that [reality] erroneously sees what is faultless as erroneous;
for Maheśvara alone exists, established through the differentiation of all causal agents. ||422||
It cannot acquire a different form merely through a difference in its causal factors;
for it is by that very form in which it is apprehended that it exists in the ultimate sense. (423)
One born of noble family attains the state of being a grasper; such is the course of existence.
Then, through the thorough knowledge of non-duality, one whose every stain has been destroyed [attains liberation]. 424.
It is indeed stainless and motionless, like a lamp in a windless house, having attained perfection through the enjoyment of its previous desires and through prosperity. (425)
Though possessing a supreme form, he who is omnipresent enjoys all accomplishments;
therefore, he is neither stationary, nor dead, nor born, nor obscured. 426.
An entity does not exist in the ultimate sense in an inexpressible form;
for how can that which is unborn exist, and if it does not exist, how can there be its persistence? (427)

How can there be destruction for that which is not abiding? These two are mutually contradictory: how could there be the arising of that which has been destroyed, and for that which arises, stability is established? (428)
The statement regarding the destruction of that which has stability involves no contradiction whatsoever;
for there is no knowledge that is the effect of anything, nor is there any cause of anything. (429)

For both [subject and object], there is no state of being a single entity, nor is there any effect or cause; it is only for the sake of conventional usage that knowledge and the knowable are established here by their very nature. //430//
Because it is dependent on that [perception], once [the object] has perished,
this worldly convention regarding jars and so forth, which are within the range of the senses, remains as something inexpressible.
How is it that speech does not proceed here in the state beyond conceptual proliferation?
This conventional discourse regarding the Yoginī is further chanted as mantra. (432)
The world has no authority here; it proceeds like one in the middle of a street.
Brahmā has no authority over Viṣṇu, nor Viṣṇu over Rudra, nor even Rudra over Īśvara.
Even Īśvara is established in Śiva, and he too is established in the Supreme Self;
then that is the supreme secret, then that is the supreme state.
Where there is no contradiction through the reasoning of authoritative speech, that knowledge arising from sense objects is understood to be perception (pratyakṣa). 435.
And since inference is preceded by that [perception], how can there be the apprehension of those two [the past and future] therein?
It would be as if one were to go from one village to another and abandon the intermediate region. (436)
In the same way, by abandoning the deities, one shall gradually attain that state;
for the word of the Guru is the means characterized by the attainment of that state. (437)
This is indeed not the valid cognition of yogins arising from the eye and other senses;
this most wonderful secret has been told to you, O Goddess. (438)
There is nothing higher than this as a means for liberation itself.
The Goddess said:
[It is] that which resides in the Bindu, that which resides in the Nāda, that which resides in the Cāra, and that which moves through the six paths. 439.
O Śambhu, there is another [state] which has entered the utterance of power (śakti), which involves the abandonment of causes and reaches the [final] time;
it has entered the state of emptiness, resides in the heart, and is established in power.
All that has been specifically brought down [into manifestation] while abiding in its own essential nature (svarūpa);
now, how does it come to abide within the phonemes (varṇa)? || 441 ||
Bhairava said:
O large-eyed one, listen; I shall describe that which resides within the phonemes (varṇas).
The Mātṛkā situated in the three wheels must be known by the wise. 442.
Those sixteen vowels which have been enumerated are these sixteen great winds;
they constitute the wheel with sixteen spokes, kindled by fire and wind.
O lady of excellent vows, she who is white and stands upon the pericarp, joined with Śakti,
emerges from the five voids in the form of an autumnal lamp-flame.
Furthermore, O Goddess, at the *dvādaśānta* [the end of the twelve], she is like a blazing sun;
there that power (*śakti*) is dissolved, being beyond the mind (*amanaskā*) and transcending the mind (*manonmanī*). (445)

O Goddess of the gods, as long as the supreme practitioner remains even for the duration of a single blink of an eye, so long will the immobilization (stobha) quickly occur; he binds the mudrās in many ways.
And at that very moment, he causes various forms of speech, the many kinds of Dharmaśāstras, and all the scriptures beginning with the Vedas to resound.
When questioned, he also speaks of the past and the future; by flying through the expanse of the sky, he becomes a lord of the Vidyādharas. 448.
Excluding the group of neuter vowels, it is declared to have twelve spokes; through the conjunction of thirty-two syllables, it is celebrated as the Great Wheel (Mahācakra).
In this way, all the *mātṛkās* have entered the three wheels; in the center of the heart is the twelve-spoked [wheel], where the sun is established. (450)
In the palate is the sixteen-spoked [lotus] where that [channel] bringing nectar resides; on the head is the one consisting of all phonemes, endowed with thirty-two petals.

Arising is to be known as occurring in the heart-cakra; separation resides in the piercing-cakra; and dissolution, which should be understood by those who have realized the Self, resides in the head-cakra. 452.
O Goddess, grasping is situated in the region of the navel, and unification is based in the throat; yoga, moreover, occurs therein, as well as in the stainless state of dissolution.

Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one should unite [the self] with the eternal state; the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) resides in the heart, while knowledge (vidyā) rests upon the pendant [neck]. 454.

O beloved, the Śiva-principle is situated in dissolution and has entered the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); it was previously described as being established within Śakti, according to its position on the path.
Now, O beloved, I shall tell you how the Lord of the World resides within each individual phoneme as it abides in its power (śakti). 456.
For those who desire victory, the accomplishment of mantra occurs swiftly through the sequence of the wheel-mālā; O Lord of the World, I shall explain exactly how the worlds are situated.

Their pervasion according to their respective functions within the spheres of the castes is established as it truly is; O Mistress of the Gods, hear now from me their all-pervasiveness and their movement. 458.
The knowledge of the Self, Śiva, and the threefold division of the principles (tattvas), as well as the renunciation of the causes as they exist according to each respective caste (varṇa). || 459 ||
Regarding those wheels previously proclaimed as being called Fire, Sun, and Moon—the Yoginīs that pervade them are situated separately; listen to how. (460)
Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Jvālā, Tejasā, Tejavarcasā, Tejormiṇī, as well as Tejas and Tejavatī, the dispeller of darkness (Tamopahā). 461.
The Yoginīs residing in the fire-wheel (agnicakra) are declared to be the treasury of splendor (tejonidhi); born from the form of the fire of time (kālāgni), they withdraw the entire universe.
Now hear of the yoginīs born from the solar wheel: Sūryā, Sūryavatī, Kāntā, Svadhā, Svasti, and likewise Sudhā. (463)
