Sumanā, Conmanā, Kāntā, Śāśvatī, and another, Saṃvartā, and Saṃharī—these Yoginīs reside upon the solar wheel.
She is to be known in the second enclosure; in the third, I shall tell you of her: Śaśinī, Śāśvatī, Śāntā, Sevanī, and Śaśiprabhā. (465)
Śītā, Śītavahā, Kāntā, Pṛthvī, Priyakārikā, Pṛthivī, Pārthivī, Prītā, Kṣobhaṇī, Kṣubhitā, and Kṣayā. || 466 ||
But in each and every wheel, the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśī) is to be seen, established in her station. ||467||
O lady of beautiful hips, those Rudras who, together with the Rudra-shaktis and the yogins, are never-falling (acyuta), sport with the lords of the worlds.
O Leader of the Gods, their number cannot be known through differentiation, even when divided by the distinction between moon and sun, or into tens of millions upon tens of millions.
There they all sport, those who bring about birth and maintenance; each one is as described, situated within wheel after wheel.
I have briefly declared their pervasive power according to the Kaula tradition; the wheels (cakras) are remembered as beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the final letter 'Kṣa'.
Fifty cakras have indeed been described, by which the entire world is pervaded; all of them, O fair-faced one, should be known as residing within Śakti. 472.
Without them, mantras would not exist for the accomplishment of visible and invisible purposes. Having uttered each individual syllable, it is differentiated by the twelve vowels. (473)
Joined with Anila and Anala and adorned with Bindu, one should contemplate the form of radiant energy there as Ātman, Śakti, and Śiva. (474)
All this has become liquefied and dissolved into the locus of power (śaktisthāna), resembling quivering rays and blazing like ten million flashes of lightning.
When one attains absorption into that which resembles the rays of the rising sun and is devoid of both decay and non-decay, then the knowledge of time arises.
Abiding in the state of Sadāśiva, one perceives with the divine eye the sixfold path (ṣaḍvidhādhvan), beginning with the worlds (bhuvana), O Great Goddess, O Beloved. (477)
By the power of this wheel, he sees everything situated below; within six months he will swiftly fly upward—this is the truth, there is no doubt. (478)
O Mahāgaurī, this wheel has not been told by me to anyone; it has been fully explained to you, O Goddess—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (479)
O fair-faced one, this secret is more secret than the secret; it must be guarded. It should never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who is not a son.
Those who delight in other scriptures, those who maintain hypocritical vows, those who are devotees of other deities, as well as the deceitful, the impotent, and those who are mercenaries; ||481||

O woman of excellent complexion, those who are devoted to hypocrisy and crookedness, who revile the practice of non-duality, and who are possessed of these very great faults—[they are not to be honored]. (482)
One should not cause them to receive the Kaulika knowledge, which is more venerable than a guru; O you of pleasant vows, he who gives the Tantric tradition out of negligence [incurs sin].

In this context, even a bound soul (paśu) situated in the midst of the host of Yoginīs becomes an adept (sādhaka). When he perceives a disciple who is devoted, firm in his vows, and has approached him for instruction... (484)

O lady of excellent limbs, having thus recognized the disciple as one who is devoted to his guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, and who is dedicated to pure vows, he should be known as truly distinguished.

At the time of initiation, one should examine [the candidate] in due order by means of the paralysis of the fetters (*pāśastobha*) and other such methods. Furthermore, that [initiation] is proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to the specific manner of falling [into the state of grace]. ||486||

I shall first describe the supreme, the most excellent of the middling; then, once the disciple has been examined, [the initiation should take place] in the presence of the Guru, the deity, and the fire. 487.
One should cause them to hear the pledges and those things enjoined in the scriptures; then, having bestowed the empowerment, one should transmit the oral instructions.
O lady of excellent vows, as it is with one, so it is with all fifty wheels; O sinless one, they are joined with wind and fire, arranged in both regular and irregular order.
When the *mātṛkā* is equalized with the source (*yoni*) and worshipped by one who performs all rites, that person obtains the threefold accomplishment. (490)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Section on the Yoga of Inquiry," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of seventy million verses belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava current. [The Third Chapter: The Section on the Determination of Mantras] [The Sequence from Na to Pha] The Goddess said: "O All-pervasive Lord, regarding this purification of mantra which has been proclaimed through the meaning of the syllables and so forth—by means of that purification, for whom is the instrument (the means) brought into operation? (96)
Therefore, explain the mantras that follow the path of the lineage-discipline, arising from the root-mantra of the limbs of Brahmā, by which this [practice] may become fruitful. (97)
Bhairava said: Hereafter, O fair-faced goddess, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra), the ritual procedure for the subduing of the Kula, in great detail. 98.
Having drawn a square city divided into seven parts,
and having multiplied it by seven again, O Dear One, one should cause the compartments to be made.
One should practice the circle of vowels according to the prescribed rule, beginning from the northeast (īśāna) and so forth, until one is short by only one [vowel] out of fifty. 100.
At its end, however, those touches [proceed] until they reach the center;
there, O God, is the Great-Souled One who has reached the station of Brahmā and is known as Haṃsa.
The king of mantras known as Kaṣā is understood through conjunction;
when the ritual placement has been performed in this way, O Goddess, one should extract the auspicious Mālinī.
Listen to how it exists in the form of the letters from *na* to *pha*:
one should fashion the head of the Goddess between *ai* and *da*, endowed with auspicious characteristics. (103)

The *pa*, *dha*, and *ma* in the middle, along with the *śikhā* (top-knot) and the *adhaḥ-śiras* (downward-head) situated below, together with the four vowels beginning with *e*, are declared to be the *śiromālā* (garland of the head). 104.
The third eye should be made, O beloved, situated between *ṅa* and *cha*;
it should be known as being between *na* and *da*, existing in two ways, O fair-faced one. (105)
The two eyes of the Goddess are to be remembered as being in the right and left [positions] respectively.
The nose, preceded by the letter *ṭa*, should be known as situated in the middle of the nostrils and closely joined. 106.
Taking the letter *ḍha* situated between *ta* and *ma*, it is uttered with a double repetition;
joined with *ṭha* and *ḍa* preceding them, they are known as ornaments at the bottom of the ears. (107)
O Vīranāyikā, the face of the Goddess is situated here between the left and right channels, according to how they have arisen.

The Visarga and the letter Kha situated in the middle, joined again with the letters between Ka and Ga; then the letter following the last of Kha is taught, as well as the one immediately following it. 109.
One should extract the auspicious syllable situated within the letter Gha;
these five letters are traditionally taught as the teeth of the Goddess. 110.
The letter preceding *rasanā* (the letter *a*) is proclaimed; with the letter preceding *ja* (*i*), it becomes Sarasvatī.
The letter situated between *śa* and *ta* (*ṣa*) is the throat; one should extract the letter situated between *ma* and *cha* (*ya*). 111.
Similarly, two auspicious syllables situated in the middle of the *ra* and *ma* are known as the "peaks" (*śikhara*);
O Blessed One, these two auspicious ones are located on the left and right. (112)
The two [syllables] *ra* and *ṭha* are in the south; those in the arms are the left and right.
One should likewise conceive of that which is situated between *ra* and *u* as being divided into two.
O Goddess, the two palms are known as *savya* (left) and *asavya* (right) by those who understand;
likewise, the auspicious fingers beginning with *bha* and *ma* are situated on the left and right respectively. 114.
Taking [the syllable] situated between *ja* and *ṭha*, one should fashion it in the left hand as a skull-cup with its opening facing upward, filled with that which is called nectar (*amṛta*).

O auspicious lady, it should be known that the staff of the trident is situated between the letters *ya* and *ḍha* on the right hand; this has been extracted according to the method of extraction. 116.
The trident situated in the middle of the letter *A* is turned upward with its tip facing up;
it should be understood by the wise according to its characteristics as they have been described. 117.
The heart of the Goddess, which fulfills all desires, is situated between *gha* and *na*;
and the belly, O Dear One, is situated between *na* and *sa*, and between *ca* and *ja*.
Likewise, the two syllables situated in the *ra-v* junction consist of the breasts;
that which precedes *jha* should be known as milk, which is proclaimed to be nectar (*amṛta*). || 119 ||
O Goddess, O Leader of Heroes, the vital breath (prāṇa) situated between *ya* and *śa* is the Self (*ātman*), which is the nectar-seed (*bījāmṛta*) situated between *ma* and *ṣa*. 120.
One should fashion the supreme mantra known as Kaṣa, which includes the *visarga* and is extracted from the Rudra [section], as the navel of the Goddess. || 121 ||
O Goddess, the middle of *bha* is known as the waist; the entire self is the hip.
That which is situated between *va* and *ṣa* is the secret place, joined with the end of *da*. || 122 ||
O sinless one, the two seed-syllables situated between *ṇa* and *tha* form the thighs;
the two beautiful knees are the seed-syllables located to the right of *ta* and *tha*. (123)
O auspicious-eyed one, those moving to the left and right should be known in their respective order;
the two located to the west of Ai and Tha are the two shanks, left and right. (124)
O Goddess, the two seed-syllables situated between *tha* and *dha*, and likewise between *ṅa* and *ṣa*, are to be extracted; O Blessed One, they should be known as the feet by the wise. 125.
The two [lines] on the left and right are said to be distinguished by their specific characteristics;
thus, O Beloved, Mālinī has been extracted according to the correct procedure. 126.
Of the seventy million vidyās and mantras of immeasurable power, Mālinī is their one supreme source, granting all desires.
Because she remained there having formed a garland (mālayitvā), she is known as Mālinī;
those who have been born and those who will be born, O lady of beautiful countenance, are immeasurable.
She is said to be like a mother to the Rudras and the Yoginīs;
she is without color, yet a combination of colors, O fair-faced one—thus she should be known. 129.
Mantras consist of all the phonemes (varṇa), and the phonemes are traditionally held to be of the nature of power (śakti).
Power, moreover, is declared to be Mātṛkā; she should be known as being of the nature of Śiva. (130)
O beautiful one, this measure of mantras has been told to you;
this is declared to be the foremost and must be guarded with great effort. (131)
The procedure for the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra) has been previously stated in another scripture.
The Goddess said:

The Ninth Chapter: The Authority on the Initiation of the Samaya. Today my birth has become fruitful, since you, the bestower of boons, have appeared before me; everything that was indicated and proclaimed by you has been fully comprehended.
O Śambhu, initiation has indeed been indicated by you, yet it has not been made explicit;
now [explain] the initiatory rite for the initiate (sāmayī-dīkṣā) as well as the paralysis of the bonds (pāśastobha). || 2 ||
O Śambhu, for men there is another rite called Tulā, as well as Prasannā, Āveśa, and Māṇavī, which grant immediate liberation; and beyond these is Utkrānti.
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of the World, explain this to me who am bowed before you: the ritual of animal sacrifice and likewise the consecration."
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak that which was previously requested by you;
I will relate all of that out of affection for you, O leader of the gods. (5)
[Examination of the Ground] First, one who is an expert in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) should examine the ground:
it should be a site suitable for sacrifice, thick with trees, abounding in śara grass and flowers, and rich in kuśa grass.
It should be crowded with devotees of Maheśvara, or even attended by a single one;
it should be pleasant and delightful, and sloping toward the east, the northeast, or the north.
One should examine it according to its own kind and by means of the path acquired;
for colors, tastes, and likewise smells are known through their specific distinctions of genus. (8)
That which is white, sweet as honey, and fragrant with ghee is for the Brāhmaṇa;
that which is red, red-scented, and astringent bestows wealth upon the Kṣatriya.
Yellow in color, smelling like cow urine, and sweet in taste is considered the earth of Vaiśyas; black, smelling like *aguru*, and pungent in taste is considered the earth of others.
One should have it dug to the depth of one cubit and then fill it once again;
that which contains less soil is inferior, while that with an equal amount of soil is middling. (11)
Where the soil is abundant, that ground grants all desires;
one should dig it down either to the water-level, or to the depth of a man's height, or even to the neck.

Just as one would carefully clean a piece of wood—from the heart, navel, waist, and down to the knees—that is free from defects such as splinters and devoid of husks and thorns, so too should one cleanse [the body]. 13.
One should diligently construct it with thorns, charcoal, and splinters;
first, one should fill it with clay and then strike it at the opening with hammers made of *aśvattha* wood.
One should smear with cow dung an area that is level, measuring five cubits, or seven, nine, or eleven cubits.
The knower of mantras should select a site measuring thirteen cubits, or fifteen cubits, or half of that, for the sacrificial hall.
Having made it square and even on all sides, free from unevenness and banners, one should divide it into nine parts by means of threads extending toward the east and north.
O Goddess, having set aside two parts in each of the four directions, one should place the foundation-slab in the corners.
One should erect pillars as high as a man, equipped with water-jars so that no vital point (*marman*) may be pierced, and provided with diamond-gems for their secure grasping.
At the front, lotuses should be carved upon the balance-beam (tulā) and provided with great weights; one should then place the object to be weighed upon the upper end of that beam.
One should set up supporting pillars above, each one and a half parts in height; then one should provide cross-beams (upatulās) with a width equal to their own internal interval.
The covering, equal in measure to that [pedestal], should extend up to the upper part of the jar; one should adorn it on all sides with the splendors of banners and flags. || 22 ||
The walls on all sides have a height equal to one-third and one-half [of the total], and it is beautifully adorned in all directions with variegated lattices and windows.
The western door, which is the most excellent, should be made equal to one part in the middle; it should be raised two parts in height and provided with a door-leaf and a bolt.
Outside the walls, a vedikā (platform) should be constructed, measuring one part; it should be made half a part in height for the sake of beauty. || 25 ||
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed according to the prescribed rule—either with baked bricks, thatched with grass, or covered with stone—one should commence the work on the ground.
Linseed husks, as well as buttermilk, the bark of the five milk-exuding trees, the three myrobalans (triphalā), the heartwood of the Bījaka tree, and likewise Khadira wood; || 27 ||
Having moistened it with these very [substances], one should sprinkle it again and again; then, O Goddess, one should pound it until it becomes soft.
The auspicious eastern direction, resembling the surface of a mirror, or the northeastern direction, should be made for the accomplishment of all desires. (29)
Having smeared it again, one should rub it with leaf-patterns and the like; having fashioned the mandala as before, the most excellent Sarvatobhadra.
Or on the eighth day, or the one called Bhūta (the fourteenth), or the full moon, or the seventh; or the tenth, or the ninth, or the third, or the twelfth, O beloved.
One should have an auspicious maṇḍala constructed during the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight, in summer, or in spring, or in winter, or in autumn. || 32 ||
The great heroes who have approached you with devotion and pure vows must be tested according to the instructions prescribed in the scriptures. (33)
A Śūdra [attains it] in twelve years, a Vaiśya in nine, a Kṣatriya in six years, and a Brāhmaṇa in half of that time.
A low-caste man in a high-caste task, and a high-caste man in a low-caste task—one should thus diligently examine [the suitability] through various means. (35)
Those who have crossed the ocean of examination are indeed fit for the sacrifice of Śiva; you must bestow grace upon them, for they are worthy of the fruit.
But those who are contrary must be avoided; they are not vessels for accomplishment. Those not born into the family of Yoginīs do not perceive that subtle state. (37)
For one who has obtained [the mantra] may thus become bewildered through negligence; having understood this, the high-minded one approached the portion of the mantra. (38)
When the Vāstuyāga has been performed, there should then follow the Astrayāga; at its conclusion, however, comes the Gaṇayāga, and after that, again, the Śriyāyāga.
Then, having restrained his senses, on the following day, he should first offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed sequence of ritual stages.
Having commenced the sacrifice at night and having gathered all the necessary materials, he should worship there the Lord of Gods, the soul of all, who possesses great splendor.
O beloved, [he saw] the supreme goddess, who consists of all syllables, seated upon his lap—lotus-handed, of great body, peaceful in form, and bestowing boons.
Drinking divine wine and laughing with great intensity, one should worship the group of Mother-goddesses (Vargamātṛgaṇa) outside, as previously described. || 43 ||
Having offered various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), one should satisfy [the deity] with wine and liquor; having thus performed the worship, one should then address the Supreme Lord.
O Lord, may that which was done by me for the sake of the sacrificial animal be flawless; O God, may all of that become fruitful through the grace of your feet. (45)
Having gone near the fire, he should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *śiva*, exactly as before.
One should perform the offering without deliberation by means of five sets of five oblations; once the path is purified, thereafter perform the sacrifice as before. (47)
O Dear One, one should satisfy the lords of the maṇḍala as well as the host of Vidyās and Mantras; likewise, one should worship the Path within the water-pot. 48.
On the sacrificial ground, in the water-pot, in the fire, and especially within oneself, the wise should perform the ritual procedure in a manner that is consistent [with the tradition]. 49.

But the undivided [form], as previously described, should be accomplished while remaining within the sacrifice; thereafter, one should cause the disciple to enter, with flowers in hand and well-restrained.
To the western side of the deity, he should cause the disciple to cast flowers; then, having prostrated before the deity, he should go near the fire.

Having meditated upon the path with the mind, one should cause it to enter the body; this libation is for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity, O lady of excellent vows, for all the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa'.
The practitioner of mantras should indeed cook a sacrificial oblation (caru) with milk from a cow that has recently calved, using Śyāmāka rice grains, O Goddess, or with Nīvāra or Priyaṅgu grains.
O Goddess, [one should offer] sixty grains of śāli rice, or else barley, wheat, and vrīhi rice; [the vessel may be] made of copper, gold, silver, or even of clay.
One should wash [the vessel], which is very firm, free of flaws, and smooth, with the root-mantra; then, taking a firebrand in the Śiva-fire, one should kindle it both outside and inside.
Having performed the protective rites and being composed in mind, he should cook it on that fire; then, having prepared a vessel smeared with ghee and filled with milk.
One should place it in the midst of the fire so that it becomes perfectly steady; one should perform its movement with the root mantra and its stirring by means of that same mantra.

When it has been steamed, one should perform the sprinkling with warm water while reciting the root mantra; when it has cooled, one should perform the sprinkling with cold water and the ritual of descent (avatāraṇa).
One should perform the sprinkling and washing with the root mantra; having brought the residual drops (saṃpāta) to the heart, one should divide them into four parts.
First, [the offering] should be given upon the sacrificial ground; second, to the water-jar; third, to the bali and the fire; and fourth, to oneself.

One should present the food offering (naivedya) and the sacrificial oblation (bali) from three locations outside; [these are for] the children, the Mothers, and the guardians of the field and the spirits (bhūta).
Having thus satisfied [the deities] and then carefully performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should bow down to the God and then dismiss him with a well-composed mind.

O beloved, together with the practitioners and the initiated sons who have approached [the rite], one should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the sequence of the ritual procedure.

Having consumed the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the prescribed rule and sipped water for purification with a well-concentrated mind, he should then take a tooth-stick that contains milk and is free from knots.
O fair-faced one, the single-sided cymbal (tāla) should be made straight, smooth, even, and beautiful, with a circumference equal to that of the little finger, and fashioned from udumbara wood.
Alternatively, one should observe the falling of other [fruits] as well— those that are rich in sap and endowed with flowers— to determine whether it is auspicious or inauspicious.
That face which falls toward the east or the north is considered most excellent;
the opposite of that is called the reverse, as observed by one who is diligent.
Through auspicious [dreams] one attains success, but through inauspicious ones, the opposite occurs; O Dear One, the mantra-practitioner should sleep during the night together with his companions.
Having gone at the clear dawn and performed the morning twilight worship,
and having paid homage to the gods and the ancestors, he should come into the presence of Garuḍa.

O Goddess, one should report the dream, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; having indicated success through auspicious dreams, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) for those that are inauspicious.
By acting thus, there will be peace and the pacification of obstacles; one should observe auspicious or inauspicious signs in dreams at the beginning of an undertaking and at its conclusion.
O fair-faced one, I shall describe auspicious dreams as well as inauspicious ones: drinking wine and eating fish and meat in a dream [are inauspicious]. (72)
There was the smearing of excrement with worms, bathing in blood, the eating of curd-rice, and the smearing of white garments. || 73 ||
A white parasol situated above his head, adorned with white garlands and wreaths, a lion-throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, and the royal consecration.
Seeing one radiant with ornaments made of precious gems, a betel nut, and the vision of Śrī-Sarasvatī, as well as the embrace of an auspicious noble woman. (75)
Having held a conversation with kings, sages, gods, siddhas, vidyādharas, and hosts of gaṇas, as well as with teachers, one attains success in a dream. || 76 ||
Crossing rivers and oceans, traveling through the sky, as well as seeing a corpse, weeping, and a blazing fire. (77)
The sighting of planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as the sun and the moon; likewise, ascending a mansion or even to the pinnacle of a palace. (78)
Riding upon elephants, horses, and bulls; climbing trees and mountain peaks; traveling by celestial chariot; and beholding perfected beings and humans. || 79 ||
There is the attainment of gains through the practice of siddhis, as well as the vision of goddesses;
furthermore, there are the pill, the wooden staff, the sword, the sandals, and the yellow pigment (rocanā).
The sacred thread, collyrium, nectar, mercury, medicinal herbs, a spear, a water-pot, a lotus, a rosary, and realgar; || 81 ||

Whatever substances that have been perfected by mantras blaze up, and whatever minerals ending with red ochre (gairika) are seen, one attains success at the end of the dream; likewise, whatever medicinal herb brings about the acquisition of land is also effective.
In the battle that was an ocean of blood, there was a crossing and victory in the fight; in the beautiful, blazing cremation ground, surrounded by heroes and lords of heroes. || 83 ||
And having obtained the accomplishment of the heroic vetāla, the sale of human flesh, and the distribution of the great sacrificial animal from the goddesses with respect, [he departed]. (84)
Worshipping the Lord as his own self, reciting prayers, meditating, offering hymns, and even making oblations into the blazing fire, he beholds Him as one who is being worshipped.
It was frequented by swans, cranes, ruddy geese, peacocks, and parrots,
and was accompanied by the Mothers, the eight Bhairavas, and the hosts of Rudras and Mantras.
Upon seeing Bhairava, Bhairavī attains success; of this there is no doubt.
Auspicious dreams have been fully described; now learn from me the inauspicious ones as well. (87)
Anointing with oil, as well as drinking [it], entering the subterranean realm (rasātala), falling into a blind well, and sinking into mud; || 88 ||
Falling from trees or mountains while traveling on the backs of bears or monkeys, or the cutting off of the nose, ears, hands, or feet. || 89 ||
The falling out of teeth and hair, the sight of bears and monkeys, the sight of cruel creatures, and the sight of vetālas and dark-complexioned men. || 90 ||
In a dream, a man embraces a woman who is dark-skinned, clad in dirty rags, covered in black garlands and garments, and has blood-red eyes.
There is no doubt that he will die if one does not perform the rite of pacification; it also portends the destruction of houses and palaces, as well as of beds, seats, and umbrellas. (92)
One should perceive one's own defeat and the theft of one's very substance among donkeys, camels, horses, jackals, and among herons, vultures, and cranes. (93)
The mounting of a crow, an owl, or a buffalo, as well as rebirth, the eating of cooked meat, and the wearing of red garlands and unguents. || 94 ||
One who has disciplined his mind sees red and black garments, and in a dream he laughs, leaps about, and wears a withered garland.
Having seen in a dream one's own flesh being cut off, being seized by a black serpent, being devoured by it, and likewise being married, one certainly does not attain success.

Thus, the inauspicious rites have been fully explained; however, the auspicious ones should be understood by the preceptor as being those that are to be approved. One should perform a hundred oblations for the inauspicious rite. || 97 ||
By offering eight superior portions of dry earth while reciting the Aghora mantra three times with controlled senses, one is liberated from the need for further expiation.
Having taken a well-rounded *karaṇī* made of cotton, one should diligently rub that *unmattā* plant with *patravālī* and other substances. (99)
One should diligently bring pure white lime from Nagara and,
having placed the thread at the Brahma-sthāna, should extend it toward the eastern direction.
Between Citrā and Svātī, one should seek the east and the west; by means of the conjunction with Uttarā and Īnā (Jyeṣṭhā), this same rule applies to the south as well. || 101 ||
Then, having divided that [line] into four parts based on the eastern thread,
O Dear One, one should form two fish-marks using that which is the fourth part.
One should establish the thread extending toward the directions, both east-west and north-south; in this way, one should subsequently establish the intermediate corners.
In the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest, respectively;
when the field has been prepared in this manner, one should then establish a square.
Once the field has been made square, one should subsequently fashion a lotus;
one should draw an excellent lotus measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
An eight-petaled lotus should be made uniform, with a prominent pericarp and filaments;
the portion for the pericarp is in the first [circle], and the filaments are in the second.

On the third [circle], one should draw the joints between the petals; on the fourth, one should draw the tips of the petals; and on the outer part of the lotus, one should draw the line of the protective wall (prativāraṇa). || 107 ||
The limbs should be made four finger-breadths in measure on the outside;
beyond that, there should be a pathway one cubit in measurement. || 108 ||
O Dear One, the doors are said to be equal to the lotus, or otherwise half of that; having thus laid out the lines with cords, one should then cast down the colored powders.
The three qualities (rajas) are declared to be red, yellow, and white;
straight, uninterrupted, and very beautiful lines should be drawn [accordingly]. || 110 ||
One should first ensure that the distance between the lines is the measure of a barley grain (*yava*);
the pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be made yellow, and the lotuses (*puṣkara*) red in color.
The filaments should be made rich in red and yellow, and the pericarp white;
O Umā, the petals are declared to be white all around.
One should cause all the intermediate petals to be red-yellow; the Bhrāmaṇī should be made yellow, and the Gātrakas red-yellow.
Just as the beauty should be fashioned in the Sarvatobhadra mandala, so too should the leafy creepers, the conch, the vine, and the svastika be made.
One should cause beautiful decorations to be made everywhere with auspicious pigments; then, in the afternoon, the mantra-practitioner, having bathed or indeed having merely rinsed his mouth... 115.
The yogin, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, enters the sacrificial ground with flowers in his hand and well-restrained. || 116 ||
Then one should worship the God who pervades the sky, who is both supreme and non-supreme, who bears all colors, who is peaceful, and who is characterized by the nine classes [of letters]. 117.

Having thus worshipped with effort, in due order, with offerings such as water for honor (argha) and water for the feet (pādya), [the deity] who holds a lotus in his hand, wears an even crown, and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. || 118 ||
O Dear One, one should diligently worship those known as the groups (vargas) in the place of enjoyment with perfumes, flowers, incense, oblations, and various kinds of auspicious foods. 119.
Having thus worshipped with various kinds of drinks and meats from birds and animals, both upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and likewise in the water-pot (kalaśa).
One should worship the Supreme Lord both in the sacrificial pit and within one’s own body; then, having prostrated with devotion, one should diligently summon the disciple.
One should conceive of its path, beginning from Śiva and extending as far as the earth; one should worship it with perfumes and flowers, and then cause the binding of the eyes.
One should have the eyes bound with a fine woolen cloth, cotton, or new white cloth that has its fringes intact. || 123 ||
Having placed flowers on the hand, one should enter the sacrificial mandala; O Dear One, one should cause the flower to be released in the southern part of the deity.
Whichever mantra has flowers seen fallen [upon it], one should assign to it a name preceded by that [mantra] and ending with the word "śakti. || 125 ||
That mantra should be given to him, and once given, it indeed becomes effective; then, having performed the opening of the eyes, he should prostrate with great devotion.
Then, O beloved, having performed the salutation in this manner over the water-pot, one should go near the fire and remain stationed facing the south.
Then, having taken darbha grass with unbroken tips that is very beautiful, the Guru should touch it with the treasury of mantras and then perform worship.

Having meditated upon the path with his mind, the teacher who has reached the further shore of reality may, according to his will, [liberate] bound souls by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal. 129.

For the sake of worldly enjoyment, creation proceeds by the path of emanation; for those desiring liberation, it is dissolution. Having thus understood the movement of the mind, one should perform the ritual attendance.

The creation consists of the letters from *ā* to *kṣa*, while the dissolution occurs through the arrangement starting from *kṣa*. Indeed, having placed the letter *kṣa* at the beginning, one proceeds as far as the letter *a*.

The knower of reality should always perform the reconnection within the sacrificial pit; first performing the reconnection of the channels, he should then perform the reconnection of the principles within.

Thereafter, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures, pronouncing each syllable individually, excluding the word "namaḥ" and the syllable "oṃ."
Freed from the sixfold birth and devoid of head and crest-lock, one should pierce [the centers] with the lotus-core and kindle that which is called Kuṇḍalī.

Neither should a lamp be applied to it; rather, that which is called the "coil" (kuṇḍalī) is illuminated. One should perform the grasping situated at the navel by means of the supreme emission (visarga). 135.
Having firmly grasped with his power that consciousness—which has the appearance of a woolen thread—right before him, as if it were a tuft of arka-cotton in the sky.

One should cause [the deity] to descend through its respective states: established in Brahmā, established in Viṣṇu, established in Rudra, situated in Īśvara, situated in Nāda, and situated in Śakti. || 137 ||

In each respective principle (tattva), one should cause [the soul] to undergo its birth, its sovereignty, the attainment of its enjoyments, as well as its union and its separation, all in their proper place.
Having pierced the phoneme, whether it be a reality (tattva), what is termed a word (pada), or even that which consists of a digit (kalā) or a mantra, one is led to the dvādaśānta in due order.
O lady of excellent hips, O beloved, whether it be the world or the path of the castes (varṇādhvan), one must cultivate the state of awakening through the application of renunciation.
The entire path to be purified is indeed united within the supreme Śiva—who is without defining marks, devoid of qualities, tranquil, pure, and exceedingly stainless. (141)
O all-pervading one, O upholder of qualities, O omnipresent one, O you who are beyond the mind; O you who are insentient yet supremely conscious, O you who are devoid of sound and touch! || 142 ||

In that which is non-awakening yet has the nature of awakening, devoid of qualities yet the source of qualities; formless yet possessing all forms, and insatiable yet characterized by contentment. || 143 ||

In the great yoga that is without support, the abode of all qualities that have support; in that which is without a locus, yet established in the state of being a locus; formless, yet possessing all forms.
Having performed yoga in that which is blissful and devoid of bliss, with parts and without parts, beyond time, where non-existence has become existence, and which is without support; (145)
O lady of excellent hips, by a mere contraction of the eyebrows, the practitioner who is situated at the equinox, O Great Goddess, being united with that, shall not undergo birth again. (146)
One wanders in saṃsāra for as long as one does not find unity; when the mind has attained the state of oneness, there is neither bondage nor a binder.
Just as copper, when touched by mercury, attains the state of gold, so too one who is united with the supreme reality shall never again fall into the condition of a bound soul. 148.
The great bondage is proclaimed to be sixfold according to the paths; its cause is Śakti, known as Mātṛkā, who is both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā).
The supreme [power] is said to consist of light, while the lower is considered the protector of the phonemes; and she alone is the path of phonemes, the cause of bondage for living beings. (150)
O my beloved, I shall briefly describe to you the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan): the letter *kṣa* possesses great splendor, its brilliance blazing like the fire of time (kālāgni).
One should place the agent of universal withdrawal beneath the soles of the feet; the letter *ha* is situated above them, starting from the big toes of the feet.
One should place the syllable *sa* on the two ankles, the syllable *ṣa* on the two knees, the syllable *śa* on the two collarbones, and the syllable *va* on the two vessels carrying the sound.
The letter *la* is said to be the collection of bones; the letter *ra* is called blood; the letter *ya* they call the skin; and the letter *ma* is known as the person (*puruṣa*). || 154 ||
The letter *bha* is at the joints of the knees, and likewise the letter *ba* is at the nail; the letter *pha* is to be known as resting upon the knees from above. (155)

The letter *pa* should be applied to the thighs; the letter *na* to the joints of the hips; they say the letter *dha* refers to the testicles, while the letter *da* is traditionally taught for the others. || 156 ||
The letter *tha* is situated in the middle of the *liṅga*, and the letter *ta* is the semen itself; the letter *ṇa* is in the secret region, while the letter *ḍha* is in the navel-mandala.
One should place the letter *ḍa* in the center of the navel, the letter *ṭha* likewise in the belly, the letter *ṭa* at the heart, and the letter *ña* between the breasts.
The syllable *jhakāra* is in the second [position], while *jakāra* is known as the peak (*śikhara*). O lady of excellent complexion, the other syllable, *śakāra*, is on the left and the right. (159)
One should place the letter *ca* at the wrist, the letter *ṅa* at the second [joint], the letter *gha* at the finger-joints, and thereafter the letter *ga*. (160)
O Dear One, one should place the syllable *kha* in the middle of the hands, the syllable *ka* on the left, the syllable *ṅa* at the throat, and the syllable *ma* in the middle of the palate. (161)
Having placed the letter *au* on the tip of the tongue, one should place *o* on the rows of teeth; one should place the letter *ai* on the left [nostril] and *e* on the right nostril.
The syllable *dṛ* is in the left eye, and likewise the syllable *la* in the right; the syllable *ṛ* is in the left ear, and likewise *ṛ* in the right. (163)
One should place the syllable *ū* between the eyebrows, the syllable *u* in the middle of the brow, the syllable *ī* on the forehead, and the syllable *i* in the form of a dot (*bindu*).

One should place the syllable Ā on the head and the syllable A in the sphere of the skin; having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of the paths (adhvan), one should effect the breaking of the knots (granthibheda).
By this sequential method, O fair-faced one, the path to be purified—dissolution, enjoyment, separation, and likewise conjunction—should be performed in each and every principle (tattva).
Having gradually purified everything, one should unite it with the eternal state.
The Goddess said:
O God, the initiation of color (varṇadīkṣā) has been heard by me as the supreme, more essential than the essential.
Now, I wish to hear about the initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) according to its true nature.
Bhairava said:
O Great Goddess, the initiation into reality is the essence, which faces in all directions.
I shall explain that to you; listen, O large-eyed one! Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well—169.

O fair-faced one, by the purification of these, the sixfold [set] becomes pure. Five are declared to be the organs of action (karmendriya), and beyond that are the organs of cognition (buddhīndriya). (170)
The five subtle elements (tanmātras) are to be known; now hear their characteristics: sound, touch, taste, form, and smell constitute the pentad of subtle elements. (171)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose are said by me to be the five organs of perception; hear now this definitive conclusion. (172)
Speech, the hands, the feet, and the organs of excretion and generation are proclaimed; O fair-faced one, this is indeed described as the fivefold organ of action (karmendriya). || 173 ||

Intellect, mind, and ego, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth, are to be known respectively as goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas)—the primary source arising from the gunas. 174.
The Unmanifest (avyakta) is thus described as the twenty-fifth principle; and the Puruṣa is the twenty-sixth, the discerning witness of pleasure and pain.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the knower of pleasure; whatever suffering was previously acquired, that which remains as the latent impression (vāsanā) of karma is declared to be the object of experience (bhogya). || 176 ||
By that purity, the manifold seed of existence is purified; having gradually cleansed the path according to the rule, O Goddess. (177)
O beautiful one, destiny is known as the fixed order, established in its necessity; it is the maker of time and number, and whatever is done by it is auspicious.

Since the reality (tattva) is pervaded by a digit (kalā) and remains as that which is delimited, it is for this reason called "kalā" with respect to one whose mind is inflamed by passion (rāga). || 179 ||
O Goddess, O Beloved, one who is colored by passion is overpowered by Māyā; Vidyā should be known as the faculty of discernment, for Vidyā perceives what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. 180.
A person who knows the meaning of the higher knowledge and relies upon the pure path, being presided over by the Lord, goes either upward or even further down into the abyss. ||181||
Whether it be liberation or anything else, impelled by the Lord, Sadāśiva alone is indeed the knower and the liberator of the bound souls (paśus), O Dear One. (182)
For those whose minds are overwhelmed by enjoyments and embraced by the seed of illusion (māyā), there is the pervasive and subtle Śakti who follows the nature of Śiva. 183.

Śiva, however, is declared to be all-pervading, established at the end of the thirty-six [tattvas]. Thus, O Goddess, the path should be purified in sequence according to the number of the principles (tattvas). 184.
O Goddess, these thirty-six categories, consisting of the nine principles beginning with *prakṛti* in their natural order, must be purified by the wise according to their true nature. (185)
O beautiful lady, that which is to be purified—the subtle principles (aṇu) that grant manifold enjoyments—and the triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, have been thus described. (186)
These are declared to be the primary ones that must be purified with great effort; when these are purified, O fair-faced one, the sixfold [impurity] becomes pure. (187)
O Supreme Goddess, all [the paths] should be seen as being included within the principles (tattva); now, O beautiful one, I shall describe to you the path of the powers (kalādhvan). 188.
The reality is pervaded by the *kalās*, and that reality indeed has the form of the *kalās*; Mahādeva, the omniscient Supreme Lord, is himself the form of the *kalās*. (189)
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti, as well as the supreme Śāntyatītā, are known as the Kalās beginning with Earth. || 190 ||
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā; the supreme one is known as Ūrdhvagāmī, remembered as the fulfiller of them all. || 191 ||
Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, and likewise Amṛtāmṛtā are said to be the portions of the Self belonging to Śakti; Vyāpinī and the others, however, belong to Śiva.
Pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, without protector, and without support—thus, O beautiful one, the path of the Kalās has been briefly described to you. 193.
One or another of these must be purified by the high-souled teacher; however, the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) is to be purified by means of the supreme and intermediate Vidyā.

O beautiful lady, the initiation on the path of the feet (padādhva) should be performed with the *samavidyā* mantra; those most learned in the scriptures should likewise perform the initiations for the worlds (*bhuvana*) and the rest. 195.
Beginning with Kālāgni and extending as far as Śiva, this sixfold procedure indeed applies to the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) in due order. (196)
The wise should perform the seizing, the joining, and the separation in their proper order, according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures. (197)
O Goddess, one of these must be purified with effort; having performed the consecration according to the rules by a Guru who knows the paths.

O Goddess, favor should be bestowed upon the bound souls (paśus) in due order, having understood [the process] according to their specific desires through the distinction between emanation and withdrawal. 199.
Then one is liberated, O lady of excellent hips, when the paralysis of the fetters occurs; when the paralysis of the fetters has arisen, it is not otherwise, O leader of heroes. (200)
The Goddess said:
O Lord, I have heard how initiation is established throughout the sixfold path; now I wish to hear, according to the truth, about the loosening of the bonds.
Those subtle nooses which have been described as arising from Māyā yet devoid of Māyā—being insentient and formless, there is no paralysis (stobha) of them. || 202 ||
The stobha that is performed upon the bound soul (paśu) is known as *pāśastobha*. The conscious being is bound by fetters, and these [factors] remain situated, mutually pervading one another. (203)

O Lord, by which two [of these] would there be the paralysis (stobha) of whom? [The five are] consisting of the animal (paśu) and the bond (pāśa): intoxication (mada), delusion (moha), passion (rāga), despondency (viṣāda), and withering (śoṣa). 204.
Variability of mind and that which is called joy—these seven are the innate impurities. Bondage consists of dharma and adharma; its essence abides in primordial nature (prakṛti). || 205 ||
Because it is subtle, formless, and devoid of volition, the stobha exists in all things; yet that which is liberated is the conscious field-possessor.
Therefore, there can be no *stobha* in that which is devoid of qualities and insentient. Bhairava said: "The Self is eternal, formless, devoid of qualities, and inactive. (207)

One who is a vessel for obstruction should be known as one to be purified and awakened by nature; however, the bound soul (paśu) is said to be non-conceptual, yet presided over by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma). || 208 ||
Previously, one was bound by the snares of the cage of fetters consisting of illusion; for from that [state], the single beginningless impurity (anādimala) remains established as the seed. (209)
O you of virtuous vows, having taken recourse to the field of dharma with the thought "may you sprout," the field becomes his *māyā*, which is the innate impurity of the bound soul (*paśu*).

Just as a tiny seedling of the *aśvattha* tree, having fallen into a field, rises up and grows, becoming covered with branches and trunks through its connection with the support of that field. || 211 ||
Thus, O Goddess, the impurity of the individual soul (āṇavaka-mala) is eternally dependent on Māyā; for that Māyā, being possessed of a cause, proceeds from the individual soul.
O Goddess of the gods, for one who is signless (animitta), māyā never arises; even so, O Bhava, the pure path (śuddhādhvan) does not proceed.
O Goddess, Śiva does not exist; at that time there would be only Māyā.
Since she arises from the nature of bondage, there is no liberation for anyone therein. (214)
O Supreme Goddess, even for those such as the Vidyeshas who are remembered by the gods as attaining liberation, this yoga may proceed incorrectly according to their application.
Liberation does not occur for them as long as the signless state does not arise; it would be as if liberation did not exist even when the true path is present. || 216 ||

When the meaning of the scriptures has not been critically examined, there arises the path of bondage known as "illusion" (māyā), just as a bond proceeds toward imprisonment when a king is at fault. || 217 ||
Just as there can be no bondage in that which is faultless, so too illusion does not apply [to the soul];
for the innate impurity alone is the continuous bond that serves as the substratum for men. (218)
Depending upon that, illusion proceeds as the awakener of the continuum;
once awakened by illusion, reality undergoes disjunction. || 219 ||
With consciousness intensified by *kalā*, its objects revealed by *vidyā*, and colored by *rāga*, it is joined with the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest. || 220 ||
In this way, bondage consisting of illusion would follow in the continuum;
in brief, merit and demerit are qualities that have that [continuum] as their substratum. (221)
The fetters (pāśas) are known to consist of that [māyā], and by them one remains bound; having thus understood the separation of the Self from Māyā and Śiva, [one attains liberation]. || 222 ||
Listen now to how the loosening of the bonds subsequently occurs: O Goddess, just as an insentient person bitten by a snake has their life departed, so it is here. || 223 ||
Indeed, they cause the holy ford to move and even to quiver;
for it is seen through the power of mantras—what more is there to deliberate in this matter? || 224 ||
The shaking, the quivering, the bursting, the going and coming, the entering of dead bodies, and the transformation of forms and so forth. || 225 ||
Becoming short, becoming thin, and emerging through the openings of a lattice—such are the inconceivable accomplishments (*siddhis*), O lady of excellent vows. (226)
How can there be any discussion regarding the power of mantras in the Śiva-āgama, given that the means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest have been declared by Śambhu? (227)
But among these, O illustrious lady, this direct perception is indeed the most excellent; for how could there be any other conceptual construction regarding that which is grasped by the senses? (228)
O fair-faced one, O Supreme Goddess, the bondage of the self which consists of merit and demerit must be brought to an end through initiation.
Whatever actions have been performed in the past and whatever one performs now, they are indeed destroyed by initiation; through the falling away of the physical body, one shall go to Śiva.
O Goddess of gods, those who abide with the nooses consisting of the afflictions and unrighteousness exhausted have no support by which they might remain on the path. (231)
For when the Self is freed from its bonds, O beloved, it is proclaimed to be without support; it falls and trembles, since its root has been severed.
Just as a tree, when cut by external forces, trembles on the earth and falls—of this there is no doubt—so too is the self described. || 233 ||
The wise should effect the severance of the bonds through initiation;
when that severance has occurred, then there is undoubtedly a state of paralysis (stobha). || 234 ||

What is designated as "stobha" consists of trembling, falling, and likewise remaining in a state of golden-yellow radiance, along with the practice of yoga within the stainless state—so it has been taught by Kāśyapa. (235)

In this way, there is indeed a paralysis of the noose, resulting in separation from its bonds, just as a tree that has been bound in some place by its roots reaching to the tips of its branches, O Dear One. (236)
Just as there is a falling when those [supports] are severed, so too does the embodied soul fall when released from the bonds of dharma and the rest, being deprived of its foundation. || 237 ||

"But liberation indeed comes about for him"—thus it is proclaimed in the scripture; the destruction [of bonds] through the paralysis of the fetters is established by those who have attained perfection, and that too is achieved through the observances (samvara). || 238 ||
Because the restraints are inconceivable, liberation is as clear as the destruction of physical poison when the fetters have been severed. || 239 ||

Cutting and paralyzing are declared [to be the functions], and no other conceptualization is recorded; O Goddess, those for whom initiation is merely that of the bound (pāśava) have their seeds burnt.
When his bonds have become rigid, then there is liberation without a doubt; yet they say that for all the scriptures, initiation is liberation.
And that liberation, though unseen, is accomplished by means of a visible cause; for eight conditions have been stated regarding the accomplishment of the unseen.

O Goddess of gods, liberation is not accomplished by means of dry logic nor even by millions of scriptures; rather, when paralysis (stobha) is produced through initiation, [liberation is attained]. || 243 ||
"Without *stobha* there can be no liberation; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. The Goddess said:
"His bonds, consisting of merit and demerit, are of the nature of a support. (244)
When their roots are indeed severed, then the self itself goes to liberation—eternal, constant, blissful, and facing in all directions. || 245 ||
It does not abide in that which is to be experienced, because what has been experienced is brought to exhaustion;
nor, O Lord, does the Self abide in that karma-nature once it has been experienced. (246)
That which is called "to be enjoyed" is the karma of the bound soul (paśu); the bondage arising from that is well-known.
Once that has been expiated, how can there be bondage? Being liberated from that, one enjoys the state of immortality.
Having reached mere death due to the absence of even a support, he would not remain in the body at all, since that [body] has been brought to destruction. || 248 ||
Bhairava said: "O beloved, the power that binds the bound soul (paśu) is the causal essence of the universe; by her the entire world is bound, and by her alone it is liberated. (249)
She binds those who are ignorant of her form and liberates those who have realized the Self;
indeed, she is called "Power" (Śakti) because she accomplishes the purposes of both. || 250 ||
Then its support would continue even when merit and demerit have perished, because their external conditions have ceased to exist, just as a tree persists even after it has been cut down. (251)
Just as [a body] would not fall if supported by even a single quality, so too the Self, residing within the body, remains as the support of power. || 252 ||
There is no falling away, for the individual (pudgala) is the support of power;
just as when the body has died, it may enter another city. || 253 ||
Endowed with the five elements and the thirteen instruments, the yogi quickly restores life to one whose life has departed. || 254 ||
Whether walking or running, speaking or eating, the single Self alone remains motionless even within its own body during both states. 255.
O Goddess, the individual soul (pudgala) is the support of power that bestows consciousness; she is the supreme digit (kalā), pervasive and eternally uninterrupted. 256.
Just as a sleeping person, O Goddess, might travel from one village to another, so too does the embodied being wander through the seven continents and the oceans.
One should perceive this even in one's own body: it walks, hears, and eats, yet it does not become empty when the conscious principle has departed and left it behind. (258)
O Goddess, no one goes anywhere, nor does any other thinker exist;
the Lord himself, the thinker, the white one, the support of power, perceives all. 259.

Where there is power (śakti), there is the mind (manas); the mind is situated in the wind (anila); ego (ahaṃkāra) is situated in the wind, and indeed, [the intellect] is established in the ego. || 260 ||
That [nature] should be known as threefold: characterized by goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).
That which is characterized by darkness belongs to the beings of the animal realm, and that which is characterized by passion belongs to human beings. || 261 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, among goddesses, however, it is the sattva quality that predominates;
by its power, they indeed perceive, go toward, and hear [the teachings]. (262)
And they also grasp with the mind whatever is desired, wherever it may be;
thus has Śakti been described by me as being of the nature of Śiva and endowed with activity. (263)
O Goddess, when there is the severance of that [channel], then the state of Nirmanaka arises;
of this there is no doubt, as it has been taught in the scripture. (264)
With support, there may be the attainment of the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā*;
but he who has accomplished his task through power, O fair-hipped one, enjoys the supreme state.
This has been declared as consisting of knowledge by Śambhu, the God of gods; now I shall explain its acquisition so that it may become firm for you. (266)
O lady of excellent vows, one should grasp that which transcends mantra by means of power;
through the abandonment of ritual action and knowledge, there is contemplation upon the station of Rudra.
O Supreme Goddess, cessation should be practiced there through the unnameable;
by means of the union of wind and fire, one is indeed praised, of this there is no doubt.
The grasping [of the breath] occurs at the region of the navel, which is shaped like a kadamba bud;
thereafter, it should be brought to the tip of the Śakti, bearing a series of garlands of flames.
Situated between the fire and the wind, it falls; of this there is no doubt.
One should meditate on the whirling [energy] residing in the navel, as difficult to perceive as a whirling firebrand.
The apprehension abides in the state of emptiness; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should meditate upon that which is called "mind" (manas), which has a shifting form and moves here and there. (271)
By means of the yoga of the serpent’s churning, there is no doubt that he falls here;
having meditated upon whatever form, the leader of yoga should pierce it. (272)
O Dear One, having recognized the supreme power, that transformation occurs quickly;
indeed, having performed the piercing (vedha), it becomes exactly like the form of the reality (tattva).
The stobha becomes identical with that, for the modification is indeed of that very nature;
knowing this, O Varārohā, O Suvratā, regarding that which transcends mantra.
The method of grasping [the breath] by way of yoga has been revealed in the scripture;
now listen to how it occurs through the yoga of mantra. || 275 ||
Indeed, this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śakti, namely *ha-ra-ī-ma*;
and that which is known as the seed-syllable of Śakti should be deposited upon all the limbs. (276)
One should place the mantra, adorned with the twelve vowels, within the heart-lotus;
in its center is consciousness, resembling the hibiscus flower.
One should meditate upon that wheel, impelled by the wind and ignited by fire, while reciting the mantra through the yoga of interspersing the name [of the deity]. || 278 ||
O Goddess of gods, for as long as it takes a mere blink of an eye, there is no doubt that stobha occurs;
O Goddess, one perceives oneself joined to each respective reality (tattva).
As long as he has not attained the supreme reality, so long does he perceive;
by this sequential yoga, he perceives throughout all the paths.
Alternatively, at that very moment, he causes all the scriptures to emerge;
he binds the many mudrās taught in the scriptures—of this there is no doubt. (281)
By this sequential yoga, one should effect the paralysis of the bonds;
for without knowledge, O fair-faced one, there is no paralysis, as it would be devoid of power.
He who knows the supreme power, the primordial power Manonmanī—
pierced by her, he shall go upward to that state which is free from all affliction.
The seed-syllable of the Self (Ā) situated on the hip, pressed by the staff (the letter Ḍ), is that seat;
it is mounted upon the left peak (the letter Ṣ) and adorned with an ornament (the letter Ṇ). 284.
O lady of beautiful hips, one should cause the moving and the unmoving to be stunned by means of the left ear;
likewise, one should cause the vital breath of the self to be pressed down upon the stalk of the navel.
O Goddess, one should again kindle it with the fire, and likewise with the crest;
O Beloved, one should cause the three worlds to tremble by means of the left ornament.
The left arm rests upon the hip; that posture is characterized by the pressure of a staff and is adorned with a left crest-jewel as an ornament.
The strengthening of all sentient beings is true, truly true; there is no doubt.
Now, O Goddess, listen to me as I speak of another supreme [practice] that is about to be described. (288)
One should cause the individual soul (jīva) to mount the fire and be presided over by that [deity];
likewise, it should be impelled by the wind and joined with the sixfold [mantra]. || 289 ||
O fair-faced one, that which is situated in the source (yoni) is permeated by the twelve vowels;
therein, the energy (śakti) residing in the center effects piercing, striking, and restraint.
O Goddess, the grasping must be performed by means of supreme union;
thus, when accomplished through the mantras, the grasping comes within the range of power.
Once grasped, one whose mind has gone toward Kāśyapī falls quickly;
therefore, one should effect cessation there in the supreme state beyond the yojana.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the connection of the vital breaths within the channels must be performed again; once that connection is made, it shall become exactly as it was before.
Therein, he should describe whatever has been perceived in each respective principle (tattva) in due order;
as far as that supreme principle extends, so far does he thus behold it.
One should diligently install that Vidyā according to the division of its syllables,
in the form of the letters from *na* to *pha*, and by way of the nine principles (*tattva*).
The grasping should be performed by means of the power (śakti), like a firefly by its glow;
one should bring it to the dvādaśānta and cause it to be released by means of the emission (visarga).
Perception is joined with the instruments along with those whose nature consists of the five elements;
it resides in the self, in the principles (tattvas), and in that [perceiver] again and again. || 297 ||
In that which is without marks, without qualities, peaceful, and devoid of all means; || 298 ||
This indeed is the seizing of the animal; now hear about the departure from it:
the seed at the navel and that which resides in the left breast, with great effort. (299)
In the secret place, the navel, as well as the mouth, the ears, the nose, and the eyes—these locations are joined with the letters of the classes in their respective order. (300)
One should contemplate Kuṇḍalinī, situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and having the form of a womb;
within her center is the wind known as Tejas, which is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

O Goddess, situated in the middle of the Suṣumnā and established within the Brahma-nāḍī, there is the piercing of the two Brahma-randhra apertures by means of the supreme emission (visarga). || 302 ||

There, having first fixed the mind, one should apply the meditative concentration on the object (*bhāvadhāraṇā*) at the navel, heart, throat, the end of the palate, and at the *bindu* and *nāda*, O lady of excellent vows. (303)
O beloved, one should cut [the bonds] with the king of weapons or with a razor;
one should mentally sever all the connections and bindings of the vital points.
One should visualize it being consumed by thousands of garlands of flames;
having emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), it severs all remaining bonds.
O Dear One, one who is intent on liberation should sever [the bonds] above the uvula by means of the Visarga;
one should meditate upon the Hiṣka located in the region of the throat, which destroys worldly existence. 306.
By this sequential method, one should recite the division of the words;
O virtuous lady, it proceeds through the repetition of the word-division until the end.
He causes beings to depart by the hundreds and by the thousands;
for this, O lady rich in asceticism, is indeed the seizing of the sacrificial animal and its departure. 308.
The supreme practitioner accomplishes this; truly, truly, O Goddess worshipped by the gods!
This very knowledge of the Goddess must not be told to anyone, my dear. (309)
By this [means], the sacrificial animals of the Goddess depart from the surface of the earth;
therefore, it must be kept secret, never disclosed, and always guarded. 310.
I shall now proclaim the Kṣurikā, as it is characterized by its defining marks:
the breast of the Goddess situated on the right, joined with the letter *ra* and possessing the visarga. (311)
The word should be repeated twice; then the second tooth [the letter *da*] again, joined with the right leg [the vowel *u*], and then that first syllable once more. (312)
First, having given the letter *da* joined with *ra*, the navel (*nābhi*) is joined with that;
then again, the first [letter] is joined with *dvi*. (313)
As it was before, so has the characteristic of the task been proclaimed;
and I have now described to you, O auspicious lady, the razor that severs the vital points. 314.
Then one should sever the vital point and join [the soul] to the supreme state;
now I shall describe the King of Weapons in brief. (315)
Having extracted the seed-syllable from the navel, one should cause it to be stepped upon by the staff;
below that, at the hip, one should again cause a staff to be made. || 316 ||
Then the pinnacle (śikhara) should be joined, and immediately after that,
O lady of beautiful hips, one should place the ornament beginning with the digit (kalā) upon the head of the left ear.
Thus have I fully declared this king of weapons, which is very difficult to obtain;
one should thus remember it as all-pervading, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
The utterance of the King of Mantras should indeed be performed conjoined with the Śakti;
meditating upon it as resembling a blazing fire, one should always recite it. 319.
Then, one should perform the contraction of the fingers;
thereafter, one should bend the knee, and immediately after that, the thighs.
Then, having contracted the waist and the secret place, there is the grasping situated at the navel;
likewise, it is situated in Brahmā, situated in Viṣṇu, situated in Rudra, and located in the middle of the bindu.
One should know that [the state] resides in Sound (nāda), in Power (śakti), and everywhere in the Pervasive One (vyāpinī);
it resides in the Equinox (viṣuva) and immediately thereafter in Emission (visarga). || 322 ||
Having known that which has come from the mouth of the Guru, one is liberated and causes others to be liberated;
having thus understood the path of renunciation belonging to the support of Power (śaktyādhāra), O lady of excellent vows.
Śakti is the subtle, supreme moonlight that awakens one to the highest Dharma;
O Goddess, that is the supreme knowledge which has come down through the lineage of succession.
Thus has been explained the state accompanied by its secret, which grants immediate liberation;
O auspicious lady, the method of the vital exit (utkrānti) for oneself or for another has been described.
It should be performed with knowledge and realization as demonstrated in the scriptures.
Now, I shall further explain another auspicious rite of consecration (abhiṣeka). || 326 ||
This is indeed a traditional practice, for those who are unfortunate do not obtain it.
Having thoroughly concentrated his mind, he should smear the hands of the disciple with fragrant substances.
There, one should place the Śakti-seat; then, one should set down either a jar or a conch filled with scented water and containing gold.
One should worship Soma therein, accompanied by the eight groups [of letters];
having formed it into a circle, one should utter the Śakti again and again.
Then, indeed, this [hand] of yours and the water-pot tremble;
the sound of the falling stream descends upon the head of the disciple.
By means of the continuous flow [of breath], one dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
this is perceived as a sign of realization by whomever it may be seen.
O Goddess, he alone is worshipped by the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others;
yet his very form is such that no color can be found for him.
O Lord, when one who is devoid of caste pursues a fraudulent purpose, how can his strength be known, and who is a worthy vessel for that strength? (333)
One should draw that Śakti on the ground in the form of a curved shape;
having gazed at it with unblinking eyes, one should approach her, O lady of excellent vows.
When one whose self is cultivated perceives the power of the crooked form, he who falls with a hundred [repetitions] is proclaimed as having a "swift fall" (tīvrapāta). || 335 ||
O Goddess, if the descent occurs by one thousand or even ten thousand [times], it is proclaimed as the middling [descent]. || 336 ||
O Dear One, he who falls [from his practice] after twenty thousand, thirty thousand, or even fifteen thousand revolutions is known as the lowest. || 337 ||
And here, within the lineage of Daṃśaka, I shall explain the classification of the fallen (pātas).
O Goddess, one should initiate the fallen, but one should avoid those who are free from such fall.
Those of evil soul who have fallen from their status do not deserve the fruit of initiation;
O lady of excellent vows, the mantras become the reality for those who remember their previous births.
But when these have been cultivated, this is the sign: it moves, trembles, and shakes;
and when the severing of the bonds has occurred, it falls to the surface of the earth, O Kāśyapa.
He who falls facing forward with his bonds severed is undoubtedly the highest;
he is designated as the best, while the one who falls supine is considered middling.
The horizontal fall is declared to be the lowest by Śambhu, the God of gods;
O lady of excellent hips, the subtle noose is not cut even by a knife.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, when that which arises from the pure, the dual, and the mixed perishes, then one is swiftly liberated from the snare of bonds. 343.
O Goddess of the Gods, initiation should not be performed for one who stands like a piece of wood or a stone, unless the offspring is to be devoid of human qualities.
With a forceful descent, O lady of excellent complexion, one goes to the celestial realm;
with a moderate descent, one reaches the netherworld, while with a gentle descent, one lives happily.
Thus has the causal condition been explained; he performs the paralyzing of the fetters (pāśastobha).
O Sovereign of the Gods, there is no paralysis without knowledge, nor without vigor.
The perfected yogi acts in this manner, endowed with the oral tradition;
however, he who desires to perform initiation while devoid of the oral tradition [acts wrongly]. (347)
His exertion is fruitless, and his initiation does not lead him to hell;
for, O Goddess, those who observe the vow indeed become guardians of the sacred field (kṣetrapāla).
If initiation were liberation in all the Āgamas, then initiation should be understood as occurring only when there is the paralysis of the bonds (pāśastobha). (349)
O beloved, when the physical body bound by merit and demerit falls there, he who then performs the initiation that bestows liberation is a true teacher (deśika). || 350 ||
He by whom the cage of bonds is shattered as soon as it is encountered—he is declared to be the Guru, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra. (351)
O Goddess, if one should bear the dust of his feet upon one's head,
one would be liberated at that very moment, just like the armor of a snake.
He is proclaimed as the Teacher, permeated by the true being of Śiva;
he is declared a knower of reality, who can shatter the cage of bonds.
He is declared to be the Guru, the bestower of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
[The Procedure for the Balance: Now, furthermore, I shall describe the supreme procedure for the balance. (354)
The balance beam should be made of cloth; its characteristic is now described.
The length of the two arms should be made to the measure of four cubits. || 355 ||
The width should be three cubits, and in the middle, two and a half cubits;
both should be made square and equal, and provided with three archways (toraṇas). || 356 ||
In the middle, however, a chain should be fashioned, joined with three bracelets;
the two ears should be made very firm, thick, and securely fastened at their joints. (357)
Thus, having first prepared the balance in front of the pavilion,
one should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) with perfumes, flowers, and sacred threads.
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) with many offerings of food for the lords;
on the second day, one should commence the weighing of the disciple.
Having weighed that same thread together with sand on one side and having ascertained that they are of equal measure, one should then bring it from the side of the fire.
The seizing must be performed with the power (śakti), and the joining again with the power;
having purified everything in all the paths (adhvan) in due order, step by step. 361.

Then the mantra-practitioner should apply [the practice] to both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala); for the sake of removing all impurity, he should cause it to be given in its manifold form.

From the full [vessel], one should effect fullness; according to the ritual, it shall be free from defects. Then the mantra-practitioner should cause the practitioner to ascend into the form of Śakti.
Having quickly uttered [the syllable] supported by *prāṇa* and *jīva* along with *śakti*, it is joined with the throat (*ka*), accompanied by the nasal bindu, and then illuminated by the letter *ya*.
O Goddess, when the left ear is adorned with ornaments according to one's desire, lightness occurs and it moves upward by itself. (365)
Pure and liberated from sin, he goes to the further shore; such is the purification declared by Śambhu even for the slayer of a Brahmin. (366)
Even for one who has committed the slaughter of a cow, the purification by the scales should be performed by the wise. For one thus purified by the scales, liberation is proclaimed.

[The Ritual for Prasannā]: O fair-faced one, the rite of deliverance for the deceased is prescribed for Prasannā. First, having consecrated a mirror along with a maiden, [one should perform the ritual] for the disciple. 368.

On the second day, however, the initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed in the sacrifice to Śiva; the seizing of the animal—which is one's own self—residing within the heart, must be carried out. || 369 ||
Thereafter, one should join [the disciple] to that which abides in reality for the sake of purification and bondage; like maidens with divine vision, they behold [it] as if reflected in a mirror.
O Goddess, wherever it may reside within the subtle body on the path of the worlds, one should effect its grasping principle by principle; of this there is no doubt.

As long as one is engaged in the supreme reality, for that long one perceives in this manner; but when the power has been attained through vision by means of the seed-syllable of the eye, O observer of good vows.
Then, O Goddess, having consecrated water fifty times with mantras, one should wash their eyes and show them a mirror.
There, those maidens behold the fruit of auspicious and inauspicious results; now I shall further explain another supreme rite for propitiating [the deity]. (374)

Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍikā, the bearer of Yoga! Proceed, proceed! Delude, delude! O Yogamukhī, O Yogeśvarī, O bearer of the Great Māyā! Hiri hiri! O beloved of the bhūtas! I see my own body; indeed, I hear; I smell by myself; I see all the worlds! Turu turu! Accomplish, accomplish! Svāhā!
Having become pure in the abode of Rudra, one should join [this mantra] ten thousand times. That Vidyā becomes perfected; it shall perform the ten rites. || 375 ||
Whether in the moon, the sun, a sword, a mirror, or a lamp; or on a thumb, or even in a jar; [one may see] a girl or a boy. (376)
From this, one causes sesame seeds or rice grains to be seen without doubt; indeed, when questioned, they reveal the past, the present, and the future.
Then, having returned from his studies, being pure, he should have a Rajanya woman lie down; he himself shall behold whatever is auspicious or inauspicious at the end of the dream.
Oṃ rakte raktāṅguṣṭhe ucchuṣme avatara avatara piśācini kathaya kathaya kathāpaya kathāpaya svāhā!
O fair-faced one, whether upon a sword-blade, a mirror, or a thumb, the maiden beholds everything—the fruit and lack of fruit of both the auspicious and the inauspicious. 379.
Oṃ piṅgali pāśupati mahāvidye svāhā! O Great Goddess, this vidyā performs seven kinds of rites. Oṃ rakte virakte avatara 2 mātaṅgini svāhā! Indeed, this vidyā performs ninefold rites. || 380 ||
Having consecrated one's hand seven times with the mantra, one should place it upon one's own chest; for by the power of this mantra, one indeed knows [the truth] oneself.
Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍikā! Descend, descend! Speed, speed! Svāhā!
Having fasted and become pure, one should recite this eight hundred times with excellence. At night, having descended [into a dream], she will tell whatever is auspicious or inauspicious.
Having resorted to the temple of Caṇḍikā for all vidyās whatsoever, one should perform ten thousand recitations; thereafter, one may cause the rites to be performed.
