Having thus examined the meaning of the cause for the sake of inquiry, the Self-existent One has taught the ritual of initiation in great detail, together with its secret mysteries.

To one who is initiated, tranquil, and consecrated, O beautiful one; or even to a holder of the pledges (*samayin*), a spiritual son (*putraka*), or an adept (*sādhaka*), O lady of excellent countenance. (385)
"It must not be told to one who is not qualified; this is the truth spoken by the Lord. However, it should be made heard by a kisser through a rite seen in the injunctions. (386)
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord Śambhu, the one who kisses [the disciple] shall be the authority over everything; his consecration, O Śambhu, shall be performed from the very jar together with them. (387)
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the girdle (mekhalā), the large wooden ladle (sruk), and the small wooden spoon (sruva). || 388 ||

The dimensions of the faces of the deities of the tongue and so forth, together with the sounds; the fragrance and color of the flames; likewise, the full drawing of the ladle (*sruc*); O Lord, I have this doubt regarding that which has not been told—please explain it to me. (389)
[The Characteristics of the Vases] Bhairava said:
Having procured eight vases made of gold or silver, they should be fashioned from copper or clay—firm, flawless, and auspicious. (390)
Having conch-like necks, large bellies, not being dark-complexioned, and having long-hanging lips, [the jars] should first be filled with scented water and adorned with mango sprouts. (391)
She should be depicted clothed in white garments and anointed with white sandalwood paste; adorned with white garlands, she holds jewels within her womb and possesses a full belly. (392)

One should place alkaline substances and so forth into those jars; indeed, the eight oceans ending with Garbhoda are traditionally said to reside there, along with the Vidyeśvaras and the world-protectors.
One should cause the consecration to be performed while the eight groups are collectively assigned; or else, O Dear One, the entire ritual arrangement may be performed with only one [group]. 394.
Or the consecration may be performed with a single water-pot, O lady of beautiful countenance, accomplishing all intended purposes exactly as enjoined in the scripture. (395)
It must be performed in that manner; otherwise, one becomes a vessel for faults. Then the mantra-practitioner, consecrated and anointed with white sandalwood paste, [should proceed]. (396)

Wearing white garments and adorned with garlands, he should bring [the disciple] into the presence of the deity; then, having performed a prostration, he should fall upon the ground like a staff. || 397 ||

[The Characteristics of the Fire-pit (Kuṇḍa): Having brought [the materials] near the fire, the wise one should always perform the oblation (homa), O Goddess of Gods, using either a handful (ratti) or a mere fistful (muṣṭi) [of offerings]. 398.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure, four cubits [in circumference], and have three tiers; the practitioner of mantras may have it made circular or according to his own desire, established in a divine manner. (399)

If the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) are of deficient measurement, devoid of girdles (mekhalā), or have broken and cracked rims, one should undertake the fire-oblation (homa) in such an unfavorable (viloma) manner. || 400 ||
The first girdle should have a width equal to the joint of the thumb; the second is to be known as three [joints], and the one situated above as four. || 401 ||
The womb (yoni) should be nine, seven, or twelve finger-breadths in length; its lower part resembles an elephant's lip, and its lip extends for one finger-breadth.
A triangle with a long face is beneficial for killing and driving away; it should also be employed for causing enmity, though it is devoid of [auspicious] characteristics. 403.
According to the specific rite, one should construct a sacrificial pit that bestows success, whether for daily or occasional fire-offerings, or for rites of pacification, O fair-faced one. (404)
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (hasta) in size shall be the bestower of fruits;
it should be two cubits for ten thousand oblations, and four cubits for a hundred thousand oblations.
O woman of excellent complexion, in a *prayuta*-sacrifice the [pit] should be six cubits;
and in a *koṭi*-sacrifice, it should be made very beautiful with eight cubits.
The girdles that have been prescribed for a pit measuring one cubit (hasta) should be made with double the increase up to a pit of eight cubits.
Those two auspicious *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are considered to be one cubit in length and made from *vaikaṅkata*, *śamī*-wood, *palāśa*, or *khadira*. (408)
In other cases, one should mark them with a single auspicious sign;
one should perform this during auspicious homas, and otherwise in the opposite circumstances.
They may be produced from the great Vibhītaka tree, or from Tinduka and Śālmali trees;
or they may be made from the wood of a stake, or from the bones of a donkey or human.
A wise person should, by every means and with all effort, ensure that both [the lips] are free from pride, not censured, well-formed, and not cracked, for the sake of beauty. (411)
Even if they are made from auspicious wood, sacrificial ladles and spoons that are crooked, cracked,
or deficient must be diligently avoided, even if they appear auspicious.

The *sruva* ladle has a handle made of wood and is provided with a well-shaped *sruk* spoon; it measures four *palas* in weight, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width, and the other [the *sruk*] should be two finger-breadths [in height]. || 413 ||
It is as wide as the middle finger, twenty-four finger-breadths in length, six finger-breadths in circumference, pure, and beautifully marked with a lotus. 414.
Having thus made [the ground] marked with a conch, a svastika, a vajra, and a wheel,
the mantra-practitioner should then touch it with his hand.
The knower of mantras, being well-composed, should offer oblations into the fire of Homa-Indreśvara;
he who knows the reality of the characteristics of the tongues of fire should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya). 416.
He who knows the rules for success and failure regarding the forms and colors in the fire—the fire-god Maheśvara, whose form is fire, in whom all deities reside. || 417 ||
His form consists of mantra, and his sovereignty indeed originates from Soma;
all the deities are established within the mouth of Agni.
One who knows the procedure for the seven tongues should commence the rite of homa;
he who offers oblations into the fire without knowing the distinctions between the tongues [will fail]. (419)
Whatever action he undertakes, all that shall become fruitless, even if he has satisfied [the deity] by offering oblations of clarified butter according to the ritual rules for the fire. || 420 ||
The bull-bannered Lord, together with his consort, is pleased by the sacrificer;
the flames, fanned by abundant oblations, spread as wide as the joint of a thumb.
Having become unified, they remain there by means of a small amount of oblation-fuel;
this mouth of the eater of beings (the fire) is equal in size to the sacrificial fire-pit.
With thousands of garlands of flames,
one should awaken that subterranean mouth with fires and then mark the tongue according to the prescribed rule.
The form of the deity and the specific fruit that belongs to each are established there,
with the tongues of the seizers positioned from the front to the back.
At the time of the fire offering (homa), one should diligently avoid two [flames]:
the first is the "Dharma-tongue," which is remembered as being blue in color. || 425 ||
The second, however, is Yakṣajihvā, copper-colored and of uniform luster;
the third has Saumya as its presiding deity, is white in color, and resembles nectar.
Yamajihvā is the fourth, and she is remembered as being black in color;
the fifth has Viṣṇu as her presiding deity and resembles the Atasī flower.
The sixth, however, has the Sun as its deity and is remembered as being white in color;
the seventh has all deities as its presiding deities and shines with all forms.
The first [tongue] is fruitless; the second bestows wealth;
the third gratifies the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. (429)
The fourth [offering] leads to the destruction of the lineage, while the fifth increases the family;
it brings about accomplishment in particular, for the power of Rudra has been offered in the fire.
Brahmī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, the goddess Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍā is considered the seventh. 432.
They should be known as having the form of tongues, bestowing accomplishment upon practitioners;
therefore, with every effort, a fire offering in the center is praised. (433)
When, while the oblation is being offered, the sounds produced by conchs, kettledrums, and lutes, as well as flutes and other musical instruments, are heard, that is the sign of success.
Or the voice may be like that of a donkey, a camel, a crow, or a curlew, or like the cry of a vulture or an owl;
or the sound may be for the purpose of achieving malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), even if it is intense with great smoke. (435)
If the crests take the form of serpents, birds, or wild beasts, they roar;
likewise, if they take the form of missiles, they quickly accomplish the reverse.
Those things which have the shape of parasols, the shape of banners, and resemble canopies, as well as those with the form of white and blue lotuses, are seen in the expanse of the sky. (437)
If the vajra, conch, śrīvatsa, mountain-form,
and flames are endowed with a clockwise curvature, they accomplish auspicious deeds.
Fragrant with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron, and agaru,
or with other highly perfumed substances such as jasmine and the like, even in the case of garlands.
A favorable and auspicious fragrance is known to bring about swift accomplishment;
such is the scent that arises when flesh, bone, blood, and hair are being burned. (440)
Whether the odor is extremely foul or even like excrement and urine, it should be understood by those skilled in mantras as being contrary to what is auspicious. (441)

Even if the fire is of an unusual appearance, if a very beautiful fragrance is perceived while it is being offered oblations, that should be known as a sign of accomplishment that bestows the desired object. || 442 ||
When the scent of clarified butter arises from substances that are both auspicious and inauspicious, it yields a mixed result, bestowing both desired and undesired fruits.

He who, knowing this, is a knower of mantras and performs recitation as well as fire-offerings, and who knows the reality of the parts of the time for ritual action—he shall become a partaker of the fruit of accomplishment. || 444 ||
Otherwise, for one who lacks the prescribed rules, it is indeed in vain and acts as a reversal;
even if the consecration is performed, one who is devoid of ritual action shall not achieve success in this world.
Ten colors of fire have been proclaimed, which bring victory in all undertakings:
[the first] has the luster of the rising sun, and [the second] resembles smooth lapis lazuli.
It resembles the color of clarified butter and likewise the color of lac;
it has the luster of molten iron and gold, and is similar to the hue of safflower juice.
It is like yellow orpiment and likewise smoke-colored;
it is also seen when the fire is well-kindled with abundant sacrificial fuel. || 448 ||

When the fire is smokeless and flickering, one should offer oblations for the successful completion of the rite; it should be blazing with flames that are compact and resemble clarified butter or gold. (449)
Smooth, turning clockwise, and bestowing the fruits of all desires—having thus understood [the disciple] according to the rule, the guru [should act] for the sake of the practitioner. 450.
Listen as I explain how the ritual application of the *saṃskāra* should be performed correctly:
having fashioned a noose made of thread, it should be consecrated with the *Navātman* mantra. (451)
Having recited the nine principles (navatattva), they are differentiated by means of the syllable Ā;
[they are placed] on the head, the throat, the heart, the navel, the thighs, and likewise the hips. (452)
One should apply the shanks, the ankles, and likewise the feet everywhere;
one should also place the two arms and the two hands everywhere. (453)

One should offer one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *navātman* mantra, accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*. Now I shall describe the procedure for the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
With the upper body erect, the neck straight, and the feet standing evenly placed— || 455 ||
At the location of the navel, the base of the *sruc* ladles should be placed with their mouths facing upward and level;
O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* spoon upon the *sruc*, it should likewise be positioned face-downward.
Having offered the flower at the tip of the *sucī*, O beloved, one should carefully grasp both hands together with the *darbha* grass using a fist.
O auspicious one, having grasped the right hand in front and the left behind with both fists, using the technique of upturned hands; ||458||
Then, having filled it with clarified butter, one should perform the act of self-identification:
"I alone am the supreme reality, by virtue of the distinction between the higher and the lower. (459)
For the single reality alone exists everywhere; one should not contemplate the existence of anything else.
O fair-faced one, that which has been deposited in the jar is the sixfold path.

Having placed [the sacrificial substance], which resides within Śiva and is conceived as common to all, into the fire of the mandala, one should project it onto that path, situated within the vital breath and moving through the center of the channels.
Having made the support of the vital breath even, one should place the supporting ladle;
by means of the *vasordhārā* application, one should pour [the offering] into the fire.
One should lead the base of the ladles to the region of the mouth located at the navel;
as one pours forth the stream, so should one exhale the breath.
The vital breath (prāṇa), however, attains the state of phonemes, for it consists of the sixfold path;
apart from the sixfold path, no object of knowledge exists anywhere.
Therefore, all those [phonemes] residing in the mantra are established in terms of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted;
however, the sixfold cause resides in the phoneme, while dissolution occurs in the seventh through the abandonment of the six.
The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the bindu;
the half-moon, the nirodhī, the nāda, and the upward-moving [nāda]. (466)
O Goddess, Śakti is all-pervasive, and beyond that is Samanā; O lady of excellent hips, up to the end of Samanā lies the infinite web of bonds. 467.
One should cause that which resides in the mantra and is overcome by the six causes to be abandoned;
here, Paśupati is the Self, situated in the void and perfectly pure consciousness. (468)

One who perceives the Śiva-dharma, which is the fragrance of the qualities of the Śiva-principle, having abandoned that which conforms to the bonds (pāśas), likewise perceives one's own true nature. || 469 ||
The pervasion of the self is indeed the pervasion of Śiva; otherwise, one should always contemplate those qualities such as omniscience which are all-pervading. (470)
And this pervasion by Śiva is indeed the cause within consciousness;
therefore, Śiva is recited as being the very nature of the substratum, which is peaceful. || 471 ||
For one whose self is established in the awakening of the Self, the mind becomes unmanas (beyond the mind) and graspable by the mind;
having abandoned mental activity, one should unite with the nature of pure consciousness. 472.
Then the bound soul (paśu), liberated from the ocean of existence, attains the state of Śiva; and for one who has been joined to the Supreme, one should again cause him to bathe in pure water.
As long as that substance is being offered into the fire through the aperture of the sacrificial ladle (sruk),
one should contemplate the external kumbhaka within the Supreme Reality.
Through the state of external cessation, there is a state of equal flavor (samarasa) with Śiva;
otherwise, O Goddess, it would not occur, just as the current of a river [is lost] in the ocean. (475)
Having remained in the water of the ocean, that which is born of the river becomes of equal flavor;
it does not previously undergo division, and so too the Self in the ocean of Śiva.
One should direct [the breath] for as long as it takes to fill the *sruc* ladle; by this very duration, one should practice external retention (*bahiḥ-kumbhaka*). || 477 ||
Through the state of equal flavor (samarasatva), the self becomes all-pervading within Śiva;
thereafter, one should bring forth the qualities, the six limbs, the words, and the invocations.
Just as when one has attained kingship, one is consecrated with jars [of water], and even other virtues are proclaimed by bards and others upon the surface of the earth. (479)
Likewise, when Śiva-hood has been attained, the wise man should bestow qualities [upon it]:
"Be omniscient, svāhā! and likewise, "Be completely satisfied. (480)
Thus, even though [the Self] is beginningless consciousness, exercise its sovereignty;
likewise, it possesses undiminished power by virtue of its infinite power. ||481||
Having brought about the qualities, one should recollect the root mantra:
"Oṃ hūṃ," endowed with oneself, for the Omniscient One, as the final [mantra]. (482)
One should present [the offering] with the utterance of "svāhā" through the oblation;
three, five, ten, or one [mouthful], using either sesame seeds or clarified butter. || 483 ||
Then, O observer of excellent vows, one should bestow the consecration with the root mantra;
having stirred the supreme nectar of power, one should place it upon the head of the disciple. (484)

One should indeed meditate upon [the self] entering through the fourth door, together with all that is external and internal, by means of the sharp powers of mantra through processes such as drying and burning. (485)
Their bodies were emaciated for that purpose, as was the ritual ablution;
after the completion of the initiation (dīkṣā), one should cause a flower to be placed in their hands.
Having caused the *darbha* grass to be released from the auspicious fire, the jar, and the guru,
and having performed three circumambulations, one should prostrate like a staff before them.

One who has accomplished what was to be done, with a joyful soul, having crossed over existence and being perfectly stainless, should meditate upon the peaceful one with wide-open eyes and a fully satisfied self. (488)
[The Master’s Initiation]: This initiation leading to nirvāṇa is either seedless (nirbījā) or with seed (sabījikā).
For those for whom the initiation is with seed, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣecana). || 489 ||
One should appoint someone who possesses scriptural knowledge, good character, and proper conduct to the office of a *deśika*;
likewise, one should appoint such a person to the office of an *ācārya* immediately after [attaining] Śiva-yoga through consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Having adorned five auspicious jars smeared with white sandalwood paste,
as well as the Śiva-jar, one should fill them with gems within.

[He should worship] with those purified by supernatural powers, prosperity, and so forth, filled with medicinal herbs and unbroken grains (akṣata), with white lotuses, with mouth-blowings (mukhodgāra), and joined with fresh sprouts. || 492 ||
O Great Goddess, one should place the five principles, beginning with earth, into the five jars; and furthermore, one should place the kalās there as well.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for each individual jar, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva,
and worship the god Vairava according to the sequence of universal withdrawal.
O Dear One, each individual jar should be consecrated by Bhairava, endowed with the six-limbed enclosure and joined with the union of mantras. 495.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Reality with exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], in the western, northern, southern, eastern, and northeastern directions. (496)
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
A wise person should prepare a pedestal in the northeast of the sacrificial hall.
There, having prepared a mandala, one should decorate it with swastikas and other auspicious symbols;
it should be covered above with a canopy and beautifully adorned with banners.
There, O Goddess, one should place a seat made of śrīparṇī and sandalwood;
having placed there the seat of Ananta, one should then install the child who has become the embodied form.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, standing facing the northeast,
one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [and offer] rice cooked with sour gruel while free from impurity.

Accompanied by lustration rites (nīrājana), [the worshipper should offer] balls made of clay, ashes, and cow dung, as well as sprouts of dūrvā grass, leaves of śamī, white mustard seeds, curd, and water.

O Goddess, having thus performed the rite free from impurity, one should cause the consecration to be bestowed; recollecting Śiva, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the jars of earth and the other elements. (502)
Having visualized [the deities] in sequence ending with the northeast, the preceptor, being well-composed, should be consecrated;
then, having caused him to put on another garment, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having caused [the deity] to enter the southern form, one should prepare the yoga-pīṭha;
having established [the deity] there and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should offer the office of authority.
The turban, crown, and so forth; the parasol, sandals, and fly-whisks; as well as elephants, horses, palanquins, and all other royal insignia without exception. (505)

Having given a ritual vessel, a pair of scissors, chalk, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a bundle of *darbha* grass, a book, a rosary, and so forth, he established [the recipient] in the four stages of life (*caturāśrama*). || 506 ||
"Abiding on the path of grace, you must always explain the initiation; from this day forward, you must exercise your authority by the command of Śiva. (507)
Having raised him up and taken him by the hand, one should cause him to enter the mandala; then, having knelt upon the ground, one should worship Bhairava.
Having thus informed the Blessed One, [the disciple] has been consecrated by your command, abiding on the path of the master and following your authorization. (509)
The teacher, standing before Śiva, must perform that which has come down through tradition as his duty: the exposition of the meaning of the Śiva-tattva.
Having emerged from the world, one should offer the path of the kalās into the fire; having performed the satiation of the mantras, one should offer one kalā and five oblations.

Having offered the five [oblations] into all five [fires], one should present the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Having performed the worship with the respectful offering (argha) and more, and having prostrated, one should announce [the completion] to the Lord.
Having been consecrated by me as a master, for that purpose there is the satiation with mantras; one should mark the right hand with the five limbs, beginning with the heart-mantra.
One should mark the little finger and the others with a blade of darbha grass in the auspicious fire; one should place a flower in the hand and cause it to fall before the mandala.

Having prostrated like a staff before Bhairava, the pitcher, and the fire, he—having obtained his authority, with a joyful soul, and endowed with the fruits of delight and contentment—[proceeded]. || 515 ||

That Guru is indeed equal to Śiva, bestowing the fruit of the abode of Śiva. At the conclusion of the rite of pacification (śānti), the initiation of prosperity (bhūti-dīkṣā) consists of the fruit of Sadāśiva.

That [initiation] is to be known as belonging to the Śiva-dharma, while the other is considered to belong to the world-dharma (loka-dharma). That initiation which belongs to the Śiva-dharma is proclaimed for the practitioners (sādhakas). || 517 ||

One should perform their consecration and appoint them to the status of a practitioner (sādhaka). This is the consecration of the practitioner, which occurs immediately after the initiation into the Vidyā.

That initiation of knowledge (vidyādīkṣā) exists according to the distinction of latent impressions (vāsanā); no distinction of ritual action (karma) is found for anyone established on the path. || 519 ||
All those actions that have been performed and have already passed away, having purified them according to the rule, they indeed remain as five parts (kalās). || 520 ||
At the occasion of the *yojana*, however, there is a distinction for the practitioner: one should contemplate the *prārabdha-karman* residing within that single object of perception. || 521 ||
Having uttered the entire auspicious [mantra], one should place it within the body of Sadāśiva; having meditated upon the god Sadāśiva in the form of the various divisions of Vidyā.

Through the performance of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one becomes endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest; for the attainment of these qualities like aṇimā, [one should perform it] with the root mantra using its own specific name.

Having offered the *āhuti* oblation eight times, one should consecrate that practitioner. One should place *śāntyatītā* in the fifth [position], and *śānti* subsequently in the fourth. Thus, having encased [the seed-syllables] with *śānti*, one should place the elements beginning with earth in the five [positions].

Thereafter, one should place the mantra of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) into each individual jar; having performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) with the limbs of the Vidyā, one should then place the enclosures of the Vidyā-limbs.
Then, having consecrated each individual pitcher one hundred and eight times with the mantra and placed them outside the maṇḍala, [one should establish] the seat with the syllable *praṇava*.

Having established the practitioner there, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa; having wiped him clean, one should sprinkle him with all the mantras as before using the mantra of the object to be accomplished (sādhya).
One should bathe [the disciple] facing the eastern direction with the three jars beginning with Nivṛtti; then, taking the jar of Śāntyatīta, one should sprinkle the disciple.
One should subsequently take up the *śānti* [mantra] and sprinkle with the *saṃpuṭa* [mudrā]; this is the consecration of the practitioner, both in reverse and in direct order. (530)

Having consecrated and caused [the deity] to enter, one should resort to the form of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); having prepared the seat with the syllable Om (praṇava), the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa should take place.
One should prescribe for the practitioner the qualifications, the ritual manuals of the mantra, and so forth; as well as the rosary fashioned for the mantra, the chalk, the parasol, and the sandals.
Having offered [the initiation] devoid of the uṣṇīṣa and having entered into the presence of Śiva, the practitioner should recognize the Supreme Lord as the one who has been prepared by me.
"May success be yours through the threefold devotion known to you. After this, one should recite the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhyamantra*), accompanied by water and flowers. (534)
It should be placed in his hand for the sake of the practitioner's accomplishment; having bowed to both, one should take up the mantra and fix it within the heart. (535)
With a joyful countenance, the disciple and the preceptor, likewise well-pleased, both go forth and offer libations to the collection of mantras in the fire.
Then, one should perform the libation for the Sādhya mantra with a thousand or a hundred [offerings]; having thus performed the libation, one should cause a flower to be placed in the hand.

Having fully worshipped the one who dwells in the three [states], and having performed three circumambulations and prostrated like a staff with a soul endowed with devotion, one shall obtain the fruits beginning with *aṇiman*.
Having raised up the practitioner, one should say: "O Goddess, protect the *samaya* with effort! At the conclusion of the initiation, it should be heard by the wise. (539)
Having thus completed the initiation at all times, O fair-faced one, the Guru should proclaim the rules of conduct (*samaya*) to the disciple who has been authorized and consecrated. (540)
One should not eat without having offered [the food], nor should one consume meat in an improper manner; one should avoid fruitless activity and instead perform recitation and meditation.
One should not utter the word "rere," nor likewise the words "he" or "he"; one should not look at a naked woman, nor even one whose breasts are exposed.
One should not look upon the play of animals, nor should one perform trivial acts; O woman of excellent complexion, one should not call Dhappaṭī a "Śākinī."
O Great Goddess, even a Caṇḍālī woman should not utter the word "sehārī," O lady of excellent hips, when one is established in the rite for great accomplishment, even if he is a householder. (544)
One who desires accomplishment should not engage in village-like conduct during the day; rather, one should constantly perform the rites indicated by one's own scriptures. (545)

In all matters concerning protection and purposeful action, one should not engage out of desire; one should always remain free from worldly involvement, while exercising discernment regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate.
One should never seek out worldly people in such a way that there is an impairment of one's Vedic study; one should avoid all those pursuits that cause an impairment of Vedic study. (547)
All this is useless if it contradicts one's own Vedic study; [the same applies to] bulls, cocks, peacocks, swans, and even boars. (548)
A buffalo, a human, an iguana, an owl, a vulture, and a hawk; a she-goat, a doe, likewise a ewe, a female dog, and a female jackal. (549)
The food of Śaśikā, Śalikā, and whatever other women there may be known by the wise—such meat is unfit to be eaten, even if it is only mentally loathsome.

During the nine months of the rainy season, one must not cross the shadow of the liṅga; this applies equally to the initiate (samayin), the spiritual son (putraka), the teacher (ācārya), and the practitioner (sādhaka).

One should not revile a Yoginī, nor should one ever speak ill of her, O lady of excellent hips; nor should one speak of a fisherman, a ball-player, a barbarian, a banner-bearer, or one who has empty hands, my dear. (552)
One who is deformed, suffering, a eunuch, impotent, blind, or likewise diseased; a wrestler, a bard, one of ill repute, a leper, or a leather-worker. (553)
The Jaṭṭa, the Bhuṭṭa, the Mathīra, the Kāpota who devours his own kin, the Meda, the Bhilla, the Ḍomba, and likewise another, the Bhaṇḍakāraka. || 554 ||
In this way, O woman of excellent complexion, one should not disparage other Mānavas who have not been mentioned, nor, O beautiful lady, should one revile an observer of vows who has approached. 555.
A wise man should not speak to the women of the marketplace, nor should he revile young maidens; he should not utter the name of the Goddess, nor should he place his foot upon the letter *ī*.
One should never pronounce the syllables *jhakāra* and *makāra* together as one; one should not utter any Vaibhāṣya doctrine, nor should one act with recklessness.
One must never sleep under a single tree, at a crossroads, in a field, in a cremation ground, in a forest, or in groves. (558)
One must never void excrement or urine, nor spit, nor engage in sexual intercourse, in a temple, on a riverbank, or amidst ashes or cow dung. (559)

A bedstead, a pestle, a winnowing basket, and likewise a water-pot; a grinding stone, a mortar, a hearth, a pestle, and a clod-crusher; a broom, and a boat—O lady of beautiful hips, she who has not performed worship should not step upon these, nor upon the courtyard or the threshold. O auspicious one, she who is intent on cruel deeds, deceitful, and a frequenter of deep waters, is indeed like a churning-stick, a poison, and a serpent.

A sacrificial post, a goad, an umbrella, a fruit, a spear, a mace, a conch, a discus, a club, a trident, a bell, a *ḍamaru* drum, a peacock-feather fan, a skull-bowl, a rosary, a yoga-band, a water-pot, a staff, a deerskin,
a purifying ring, an axe, a sharp-edged spear, a cheek-ornament, a hatchet, a small axe, a sickle, a spade, a hoe, and likewise a foot-stool.

The bow, the iron arrow (nārāca), the broad-headed shaft (bhalla), the crescent-headed arrow (tīrikā), the reed-arrow (śara), the *kaṃbara*, the *puṭa*, the *karṇika*, the *kūṭa*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the *vilumpaka*, the *vāvallaka*, the *asthoḍa*, the *silla*, the *ghātana*, the *daṃhikā*, the *karṇika*, the *jhaṣaka*, the spear (*kunta*), the *vasunandaka*,
the *kurttarī*, the *karttikā*, the *pādavellaka*, the *pharaka*, the sword (*khaḍga*), or any other weapon, O beloved— these should be fashioned. (566–568)

The practitioner of mantra should never touch [the vessel] with his foot, nor should he ever step over it. He should never eat from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, or *arka* trees. O sinless one, the practitioner of mantra should not eat food held in his left hand; he should give with his left hand, but cause others to give with the right.
O beloved, he should always receive what is given by another with his left hand. The practitioner of mantra should not give medicine, nor should he ever have it prepared for the sake of protection.

One should not engage in mutual chatter regarding the Śiva scriptures; yet, when established in the rules of authority, one must never speak what is not the Word. (572) One must not break the assembly of heroes (*vīragoṣṭhī*), nor should one overlook a mocker. One should never engage in contentious debate, whether with others or even with oneself.
(573) One should address all abodes of Rudra as preceded by the word "Śrī. A wise person, established in his greatness, should not utter the name of the Guru. (574)

Having left her bed and seat, and holding a flower in her hand, she should prostrate herself on the ground like a staff and utter the syllable *Śrī* at the beginning. Then, at the end, she should add the name of the deity, or the deity’s name alone; likewise for the lineage of gurus, the Siddhas, and the Ācāryas, O Maheśvarī.

Thus, O Goddess, the rules have been fully explained for those who seek the rules. The Guru himself should cause [the disciple] to hear them through the ritual prescribed in the scriptures. One should worship the Deity three times a day through the ritual perceived by meditation.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, the section on the Initiation of the Vow (*samayadīkṣā*), in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra belonging to the Bhairava stream, within the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses. [Now begins] the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Secret Signs" (*chommakādhikāra*). The Goddess said: "O Lord, I have heard specifically concerning the characteristics of the Yoginīs, the sporting of the Śākinīs, and indeed the gestures of the Sheharikas.
I have also understood specifically how their assembly occurs. Now I wish to hear about the secret signs (*chommakā*) and their language in particular."
By merely [knowing] a hundred *chommakas*, one becomes esteemed by them; for the practitioner who is devoted to *mudrās* and *chommakas*, they indeed grant success.

Bhairava said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the *chommakas*—through the touching of limbs and body parts, and through the speech and gestures of mantras—by which the Mothers converse with one another with practitioners. Listen now to that procedure, the characteristic of the *chommakas* of the limbs.

If she touches one hand with the other, it constitutes a salutation; and if she shows her ring finger, it constitutes a return salutation. (6) If she causes one hand to vibrate with the other, she intends to eat an offering; if she touches her forehead, she says, "Where am I going? (7) If she touches her navel, she says, "I am hungry"; and if she touches her breast, it is said that she means, "My mother. (8)

She who touches the elbow says, "I am going. She who lolls her tongue says, "I shall eat human flesh. She who touches the eye with a glance says, "I will not turn back. When she touches the side, it is said that there is no liberation. By touching the hair, she says, "I grant my favor. When she touches foot with foot, it is said, "I take my delight."
If she grinds her teeth, it means "Give me food. When she touches both rows of teeth with her tongue, it means "I am satisfied with this.
[12] If she touches the tips of her feet, it means "I am dying; you must not go. If she makes a sound as if snoring, it means "There is no work to be done.
[13] If she shows both hands like branches, one should show her a blue lotus (*utpala*). If she forms a hollowed cup with her hands, one should extend one's hand toward her. [14]

She who scratches her hand should scratch his forehead; she who scratches her breast should let tears fall upon her hand. She who draws lines on the ground with her big toe should let her big toe fall; she who slaps her feet together should slap her buttocks. She who sees herself anointed with oil should give him a release; she who shows the tip of her nose should show him her tongue.

If she shows her forehead, one should cause her neck to be shown; "O lofty one" (pottuṅge) is the salutation, and "O very lofty one" (prattuṅge) is the response. From showing one finger comes "welcome" (svāgatam), and from two, "very welcome" (susvāgatam). When the thumb is reflected in the hollow of the hand, it is prescribed as the "mudrā of well-being" (kṣemamudrā).
If she shows her tongue, one should show her the edge of her teeth; if she shows her head, one should show her her forehead.

If she shows her hair, one should show him the topknot; if she shows her chin, one should show him his ear. (21) If she shows her neck, one should show him his arm; if she shows her arm, one should also show him his hands. (22) If she shows her eye, one should show him his nose; and if she shows her breasts, one should also show him his belly. (23)

She who shows her hip should also show her secret place; she who shows her thigh should also show her knee. She who shows her knee should also show her shank; she who shows her shank should also show her feet.
And she who shows a frown, the Vināyakas threaten her.
To her who shows the Garuḍa, one should show the trident as well.
"Nārtha" is the greeting; "pratyānārtha" is the reply-greeting.
O highly fortunate one, my beloved, such things as these are the general secret signs.

O illustrious lady, that which was taught by me according to the literal meaning [of the syllables] is [attained] only after hundreds of millions of recitations have been performed by those devoted to physical mortification. (28)
At the time of the ultimate end, they do not reveal themselves even to ministers through fierce asceticism; rather, they bestow the supreme sacrificial oblation (caru).
They bestow assemblies where there is a meeting with happy yogins upon those who have been consecrated by the family initiation and are devoted to the family.
To them, I shall explain the secret signs (chommakas) established within the families.
Whether it be a hero or even a woman, they attain equality within the family.
Having performed the complete ritual placement (nyāsa) with Bhairava and Bhairavī,
one should enter the street of the gods when it is seen by women.
She who displays her topknot should display her head;
she who displays her head should display her forehead. (33)
She who shows her garland of heads should also show her face;
she who shows her eyes should show him her eyes. (34)
One who shows the nose should show him Ardheśa;
one who shows the third eye should show him Bhārabhūti.
She who shows the skull should show him Mahāsena; she who shows her throat should show him the Threefold Form (Trimūrti).
She who shows her teeth should show him the burden;
she who shows her tongue should show him the spreading out. || 37 ||
Lakulīśa reveals that which is shown by speech;
Ajeśa reveals it to the four-faced one (Brahmā) by showing his fingers.
She who displays the trident, she who displays the single eye, she who displays her arm, and she who displays Chaga Mahākāla. || 39 ||
She who displays her belly, she who displays a single eye, she who displays her heart, and she who also displays a ram; ||40||
To her who shows herself as the Self (Ātman), one should show Śveta;
to her who shows Prāṇa, one should show Bhṛgu. || 41 ||
She who shows her breasts shall show him a serpent;
she who shows a lotus shall show him Īśvara.
She who shows her hip should show him Dviraṇḍa;
she who shows her navel should show him Krodhīśa. || 43 ||
To her who shows the Secret, one should show Khaḍgīśa;
to her who shows the Subtle, one should show Ananta. || 44 ||
She who shows her thigh should show Umākānta;
she who shows her right shank should likewise show Raudrī.
She who shows her left calf should show him the Jyeṣṭha [mantra];
and she who shows her knee should show him the Sadyojāta [mantra]. || 46 ||
She who shows her feet, or she who shows the blood of a monitor lizard—
such are the varieties, O highly fortunate one, numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
They declare this to be a portion of the lord of practitioners; there is no doubt about it.
However, it should be understood by the mantra-practitioner for the purpose of mutual communication. 48.
Perhaps, through a divine conjunction or by the sight of field-protectors and others, they may grant an instruction; then one should certainly carry out what is prescribed with resolve. (49)
One should not transgress a divine utterance, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
this characteristic has been declared through many different modes.
It should be known that for the sake of accomplishing all siddhis, he alone is the kisser;
he is the supreme god Śiva, established here upon the surface of the earth. ||51||
A wise person should constantly bind the dust of his feet upon their heads;
the deities will always protect them and cherish them like their own children.
They do not create any flaw for him; rather, they bestow external favor.
Know that the characteristics of the field and so forth are likewise; thus one shall become beloved. 53.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Chommaka," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava stream belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, comprising seventy million verses.
The twenty-fourth chapter on the Authority of Time [Knowledge of Time]: O Dear One, the measure of the number of days within the wheel whose nature is time.
O observer of good vows, when the six days [of the week] are recited as a single group, O beloved, multiply three years by three hundred and sixty. (178)
I shall now state, in brief, the measure of the remaining portion:
two years are specified, and months numbering eleven (the number of Rudras). 179.
The measure has been told to you as exactly fifteen days;
when the wind blows on the seventh day, it carries [the fetus] away.
O beloved, two years and eleven months are declared to be the duration of life; beyond that, it is said to be the eighth [period].
If the lifespan is two years and ten months, O Goddess, he lives for two years minus nine days from the time of marriage. || 182 ||
Furthermore, for those who know the measure of time, eight months is the duration;
O Goddess, by ten days [of such signs], he lives for two years.
When the channel (nāḍī) flows for eleven days,
it is declared to be one year, with the months numbering according to the Rudras (eleven).
Twenty days have been declared, O Supreme Goddess;
by the flow of twelve such days, one year is proclaimed. (185)
O beautiful one, the months are said to be eleven in number, and the days are ten;
O Goddess, when these thirteen [days] flow during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
O beloved, he shall live for one year and ten months;
O sinless one, twenty days are also declared—thus has it been told to you.
And when the course of the days is counted as fourteen (two times seven), it is declared that the lifespan is nine months. (188)
The measure of life is indeed ten days;
by moving through fifteen days, one year is completed—of this there is no doubt. (189)
O Supreme Goddess, by the movement of two sets of eight [digits],
the life span is measured in days according to the Rudra system, and in months by their total count.
The measure is said by me to be twenty-five days, when the vital wind flows for exactly seventeen days. (191)
At that time, O beloved, its duration is said to be eleven months and twenty days; of this there is no doubt. (192)
O beloved, by means of a movement of eighteen days, there are eleven months;
the number of ten days has been declared by those who know time.
O Supreme Goddess, when twenty-one days remain in the course [of life], the lifespan there is declared to be ten months; of this there is no doubt.
Twenty days are said for those who worship the Kālacakra;
O Goddess, when twenty [days] have passed, their life is gone after six months. 195.
O Goddess, the Sun flows for twenty-one days;
he declares five months to consist of twenty-seven days. (196)
Thirty ghaṭikās are declared to be the measure;
two [periods] of twenty pādas each are arrayed, and for those whose lifespan has passed, there are five months. (197)

"O Goddess, twenty-five days for you have been declared. O Goddess, when the 'twenty-triad' (60) flows without weariness, O Beloved, these five months and twenty days are the life span. When the 'twenty-plus-four' (80) flows, O Beloved, these five months and ten days are the life span here. When twenty-five days are exhausted, he lives for three months."

O fair-faced one, the *Kālacakra* was previously explained by me in brief. Those sixteen days that were mentioned in the interval must be subtracted according to the sequence of parts; that result is made manifest. The *Kālacakra* is revealed for the awakening of those of dull intellect.

(201–202) The venerable Bhairava said: The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Authority on the Practice of the Self. O Goddess, [I shall explain] the movement of the practice of the Self, the determination of the channels (*nāḍī*) and lotuses (*padma*), the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) together with the Person (*puruṣa*). (1)
O Bhairavī, I shall describe exactly as they are situated all those [channels] beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ma*, which are well-established in groups of five.
They should be known as the openings of the channels (*nāḍīmukha*), existing in a state of mutual pervasion. The Self (*ātman*) moves eternally from station to station in successive order.
O Great Goddess, those nine lotuses which are remembered—*pha, ja, jha, ṭha, ḍha, ya, ta, tha, da*—are thus proclaimed as the nine lotuses.
One should offer the *yaralavāstu* that have been described in their proper sequence: in the northwest, the southeast, the northeast, and the southwest.
O Goddess of the Gods, the two called *haṃsa* are in the two flanks, while *śa* and *ṣa* are located at the penis and the anus; thus, in this order, the nine lotuses are proclaimed.

One should designate the central one among these as the eight-spoked lotus (*aṣṭāra-padmam*). Therein, O auspicious lady, the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) are situated, and the vital airs (*vāyavaḥ*) have them as their support.
The channels beginning with *iḍā* and ending with *śaṅkhinī*, extending from the east to the northeast (*īśa*), as well as downward and upward, are situated therein, O beautiful lady.

(8) The channel located within the interior of the lotus has the wind established in its spike (*śūla*). The winds beginning with *prāṇa* have been declared and described by me, O sinless one. (9) As for that which is called the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), it is situated in the middle of the petals; the Lord himself resides in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), endowed with the three mandalas. (10)

Fire, the sun, the moon, and likewise the fourfold power—within them, by its own radiance, exists that which has the form of a spark of fire. O Dear One, it remains under their control, situated within the belly of Kuṇḍalinī; it is like a sleeping serpent, the sleeping Amṛta-kuṇḍalinī.
Bound firmly by these bonds, the helpless [principle] of all embodied beings remains in the heart, joined with exhalation and inhalation.

O beautiful one, as far as the upward movement of that God of gods extends, so far is he remembered as pervasive; for the Lord of the universe, the effulgent one, pervades both the upper and lower regions.
(14) Established in the lower part, the God of gods, the Lord of the world, pervades [all]. The letter *A* is the heart, and Brahmā is the presiding deity there.
(15) The letter *Ī* is from the throat, O Goddess, and Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, is there. The letter *U* is to be known as being in the palate, where Rudra is established. (16)
The dot (bindu) at the *dhruva* is Maheśa, and the resonance (*nāda*) in the mouth is Sadāśiva; he who is established in authority must be known as such, which I shall explain to you.

(17) One should practice the inner sacrifice according to the former method, likewise intent upon its utterance; through the tenfold path of yoga, one should practice the Self as the independent (*svacchanda*).

(18) One should meditate with non-duality on that which is all-pervading—the measure (*mātrā*), the dot (*bindu*), that which transcends it, the essence of resonance (*nāda*), whose form is light, and which consists of the mental construction of the goal of meditation. (19)

One should fill [the breath] through the right [nostril] and exhale through the left alone; this is the purification of the channels for the path to the way of liberation. From exhalation, inhalation, and retention, the three types of prāṇāyāma are traditionally taught. These are the common external ones; furthermore, there are the internal ones. One should exhale through the internal [channel] and inhale through the internal; having performed the motionless *kumbhaka*, these are the three internal ones.

Through the movement from the navel to the heart, and from the mind to the range of the senses, the fourth type of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is known as the "well-peaceful" (supraśānta). When the retention of the breath is complete, one should lead it to the navel and remain there; then, one should slowly release the air through the left nostril. One should hold the wind-element at the thumb, the fire-element in the middle of the navel, the Mahendra-element at the region of the throat, and the Varuṇa-element resting at the uvula.
The *dhāraṇā* on space at the crown of the head is remembered as the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). It is perfected through one, two, three, four, or five *udghātas*.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained, having gone to the crown of the head, it returns; that is declared to be an *udghāta*, which should always be understood by yogis. Through the practice of *prāṇāyāmas*, passion and hatred are abandoned; through *dhāraṇās*, all sins [are destroyed]; and in *pratyāhāra*, there is the restraint of the senses.
In the heart, the anus, the navel, the throat, and likewise in all the joints, these—beginning with *prāṇa*—are established. Listen to me regarding their forms and sounds.
(29) *Prāṇa* resembles molten gold and is like the color of an *indragopaka* insect; it has the appearance of milk and the luster of crystal—this is the characteristic form of the five.
(30) The sound of the bell is sweet, like the trumpeting of an elephant and a great resonance; this is declared to be the sound of the five, beginning with *prāṇa*. (31)

Now hear concerning their external and internal movement. One should first conquer the vital breath (prāṇa); when the breath is conquered, the mind is conquered. When the mind is conquered, the peaceful-souled one shall manifest the supreme reality. (45) One should meditate on the prāṇa and apāna at the anus; the prāṇa and samāna are located in the navel; the prāṇa and udāna are in the throat; and the prāṇa and vyāna pervade the whole body. (46) One should restrain the [five winds] beginning with Nāga, which are joined with the prāṇa, within their respective locations. Listen to me as I describe the duration for that which has been restrained. (47)

It should be held from the *tāla* [measure] up until the end of the fifteenth; in this way, the vital wind (*anila*) is indeed conquered for the practices of transference (*saṃkrānti*) and egress (*utkrānti*).
(48) His divine radiance, auspicious fragrance, and wisdom increase; he gains divine vision and hearing, and divine speech proceeds forth.

(49) He may move through the worlds like the wind and behold the perfected ones (*siddhas*) and the gods; the attainment of whatever the mind desires and the eightfold qualities (*aṣṭaguṇa*) come into operation. (50)

With all desires perfectly fulfilled and free from all dualities, he becomes liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra and is equal to Śiva. (51) Having joined the prāṇa and apāna breaths together and endowed them with ten million short [units of time], the lord of yogins should hold them at the navel; then perspiration and trembling arise.
(52) Again, staying thus in the heart, one should restrain the prāṇa and apāna; through the union with ten million long [units of time], one falls to the earth at that very moment. (53)
In this very way, one should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa) situated in the throat; through the union of millions of *pluta* [protracted] breaths, one’s own activity becomes subtle (*suta*).

(54) One should effect the restraint of the vital breath by means of that which is joined with the *bindu* at the center of the eyebrows; there, deep sleep (*suṣupta*) arises, and from that moment, one awakens.

(55) Having reached the aperture at the crown of the head, one should begin the meditation on the partless (*niṣkala*); for him who practices in this manner, the sign of attainment (*pratyaya*) will then arise. (56)
From the piercing by the "ant-thorn," the gateway at the crown of the head is split open;
having pierced all [the centers] in succession, it extends as far as the end of the Transmental (unmanā).
O Goddess, having abandoned the aforementioned characteristics, the practitioner attains freedom of will;
indeed, he becomes equal to that [divine state] even with this very body. (58)
He may transfer himself into the bodies of others, and he is not afflicted by hunger or thirst;
indeed, he knows all that has passed and all that is yet to come, as it unfolds within the three worlds.
That becomes manifest to him, and omniscience arises;
thus, having known the movement of the vital breath within the bodies of all embodied beings.
Moving by means of eight petals, it again proceeds to another color; O Goddess of Gods, at the end of the letters from *ka* onwards, it brings about transformation.
Abiding in sattva, abiding in rajas, and abiding in tamas— experiencing these qualities,
O Goddess, he thus wanders, going from one place to another.
The channels resemble lotus fibers; within them the vital wind circulates.
At the thumb and the fingers, the channels are likewise situated there. (63)
The middle and ring fingers are the channel known as *ka*;
the thumb is the one known as *kha*, and by the word "and" (*ca*), the little finger is included. (64)
O lady of beautiful hips, three channels of the right hand have been indicated:
the letter *gha* is situated in the left thumb, and the letter *ha* is known to be in the middle finger. (65)
O lady of excellent vows, the *kanīyā* [artery] is indeed at the letter *A* on the left hand;
I shall now describe the channels of the feet correctly and in their proper sequence.
By the letter ṇa, however, is the little finger; the middle finger resides in the letter na. By the letter pa, the thumb is to be known; thus the triad of channels is proclaimed.
O lady of beautiful hips, it is now likewise on the left side of the right foot;
I shall describe this to you in brief, O fair-faced one. (68)
That supreme channel, Suṣumnā, which resides in the secret place and extends as far as the aperture of Brahmā, must be known by the teacher.
Mounted there, yet free from conceptualization, he moves both downward and upward;
at the palate, however, there is a sixteen-spoked wheel situated with its face turned downward.
Having reached that point, he turns back and rushes through the nostril;
having then reached the *dvādaśānta*, he enters the city once again.
Likewise, O beloved, an eight-spoked [wheel] should always be known to be in the station of the Bindu;
however, a six-spoked one is situated in the station of Śakti within the subtle path.
In the station of Brahmā, however, the supreme circle of deities is to be fully worshipped;
Viṣṇu, the Yoginī, and the Dūtī are those who reside in the station of Rudra.
O Goddess, what is to be done regarding Īśvara? O Mātṛs, in Sadāśiva and likewise in Śakti, O Queen of the Gods, one should install Viśva and the others in their proper sequence.

The first is the circle of deities (devatācakra), the second is known as the circle of yoginīs; the third, O Goddess, is the circle of messengers (dūtikā), while the fourth is that which is to be performed (kiṃkārya).
O Goddess, the Mātṛcakra is remembered as the fifth, so it is proclaimed;
O Goddess, the sixth belongs to Viśveśvarī, as has been declared by me to you. (76)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should meditate upon the six wheels within the inner self;
having attained the *kaulikī* perfection, one proceeds to the perfection of yoga. (77)
Having thus understood the movement of the breath, one should perform the piercing of creation (*sṛṣṭivedha*).
O Supreme Goddess, it is in that very wheel (*cakra*) where the piercing is indeed bestowed.
O Goddess of the gods, he perceives that wheel directly;
indeed, the consciousness of the practitioner becomes identical with it. (79)
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, the piercing of emanation is performed:
the emanation of Vāyu is in the letter *ya*, while that which is of the nature of killing is in the letter *ra*.
In the letter *la* there is the creation of the pillar; in the letter *va*, that which consists of Varuṇa;
in the letter *ha*, there is the creation of the vital breath, conjoined with the letter *sa*.
For the sake of the nectar, the best of practitioners should perform that which has been indicated;
the twenty-five [letters] beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* have been proclaimed. (82)
By means of these, the piercing of creation occurs once one has understood the divisions of desire;
thus the creation of mantra and likewise the creation of the principles (tattva) have been fully described. 83.
The creation of the individual soul has been fully described, as well as the subsequent creation of the castes;
likewise, O Goddess, the creation of the elements and the creation of yoga.
O Supreme Goddess, by meditating upon whatever form one may pierce [the target], the practitioner's own consciousness becomes of that very nature. (85)
The practitioner must understand that everything takes the form of emanation;
O Goddess of Gods, I shall now describe the five gates in brief. (86)
The hands, the feet, and likewise the secret place—these are proclaimed as the five piercings (vedhas). He who desires to perform the piercing while devoid of this path [is lost]. (87)
One might strike the sky with one's fist or drink from a mirage;
yet, there is no piercing of the nose, the ears, or the eyes in that [unconditioned state]. (88)
These are said to be the side-entrances; therefore, they are fruitless for piercing [the target] in the rites of causing hatred, expulsion, or killing. (89)

Thus, having extracted the essence from this twenty-thousand-verse tantra consisting of twelve parts, [this work] is easy to understand and free from confusion, together with its secret teachings. (90)
This has been described in detail, filled with various forms of consciousness,
by him through whom I have indeed been worshipped with devotion for thousands of births.
He indeed attains this there, whereas another, upon seeing it, becomes bewildered.
O Goddess, this supreme tantra has not been told by me to anyone.
O Goddess, this secret has been declared to you and made manifest;
it is worthy of worship by hosts of sages and gods, and is adored by the Yoginīs. (93)
There is nothing superior to this tantra, which is presided over by the power of Rudra;
for those born into the family of Yoginīs, whose minds are absorbed in that state, [this is the supreme path]. 94.
O Goddess of great renown, those who know this scripture—which contains hidden meanings and is an ocean of knowledge—know that where this Tantra is written, it remains present. 95.
They too shall attain liberation through alms-food, O fair-faced one;
for the yoginīs protect them and guard them like their own children.
No plague occurs for him, nor does anything inauspicious exist anywhere, for he who worships the scripture, which is like nectar and full of essence, O Beloved. (97)
By him [the vow] has been sacrificed to, for this has indeed been heard; he has performed the protection of the pledge.
Yet that evil-minded one, by his own intellect, does not conceive of the path of the sacred seats. (98)
They do not undergo rebirth; they go to the vicinity of Raurava.
Therefore, [one should attain] that Kaulika accomplishment which is the meaning of the mantra through the lineage. 99.
One should listen in the presence of the Guru until it becomes pure;
it must be guarded with effort and should not be disclosed to one who is unrefined.
But he who, out of negligence, causes [the text] to be heard without understanding the proper sequence, that evil-minded betrayer of his guru goes to a terrible hell. (101)
I am not his protector when he is sinking in the ocean of existence;
standing in the midst of the host of Yoginīs, the practitioner here is nothing but a beast.
O fair-faced goddess, whatever destination one who betrays his friends, his guru, or the gods goes to, that same destination he shall go to. (103)
Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, one should not act openly;
rather, one should carefully conduct an examination through many different means. (104)
Then, having bestowed the consecration, one should cause [the disciple] to hear it and have it given;
otherwise, a fault arises—such is the certainty of the scripture.
O Goddess, this supreme scripture must not be given to just anyone.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Section on Self-Conduct," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava stream belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses.
